speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 21 and 22, 25 MPs and experts from 15 countries sponsored by Parliamentarians for Global Action met in Ottawa to develop a new approach to peacekeeping.
During the recent Iraq-Kuwait war there was much talk about a new world order. That war also taught us that the existing approach to peacekeeping was no longer adequate. It is mostly ad hoc, reactive, slow and underfinanced. In the case of the Iraq war, the force was overwhelmingly American and not under UN command.
What is needed is an early warning process that will provide for preventive peacekeeping. Under such a process there would be standing UN peacekeeping forces stationed in the different regions of the world which would be sent to trouble spots to deter and repel aggression such as that of Iraq against Kuwait.
It is easier and less costly to prevent the occupation of a country than to evict an aggressor once an occupation has taken place.
I ask the government and this House to take these proposals seriously and make the slogan "a new world order" a meaningful reality.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that Canadians who say they want to separate and other Canadians who say "let them go" realize that a
divided Canada will mean a lower standard of living for all of us.
Each portion of a fractured Canada would of course assume its own share of our national debt. But each portion would also have a much more narrow economic base. That would reduce our attractiveness to the lenders who finance our debt and result in higher borrowing costs, higher taxes and less government services for all of us.
In addition, Ontario and Quebec with economies that are so closely linked by massive two-way trade would be especially hard hit if the free movement of goods and services was in any way restricted.
Perhaps some Canadians think that a lower standard of living would be worth it, but I am not one of them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government's attempt to make up for its lack of commitment to education by talking about national objectives and standards in last week's throne speech is nothing less than a charade.
Due to the government's cutbacks and the federal commitment to the provinces for education, the University of Prince Edward Island announced last week that tuition fees would need to increase by 15 per cent. This could cost students $280 more a year.
Here we have a federal government that has not increased the maximum student loan allowed since it came to office in 1984; a government that has imposed a tax on books, learning materials, further burdening students with more costs; a government that has implemented a 3 per cent administration fee on student loans, which is nothing less than a tax on the most needy students in our country.
Actions speak louder than words. We have had seven years of words. So when are we going to see some action on the part of the federal government to improve the accessibility and quality of our nation's education system?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Port of Halifax is facing the possibility of losing a considerable part of its container traffic because rail costs from Halifax to central Canada are prohibitive.
This loss will result in substantially reduced rail traffic from Atlantic Canada to central Canada and could in fact jeopardize the viability of the entire rail link to Atlantic Canada. The final result could be a devastating blow to an economy already lagging behind the rest of the country.

Under section 3 (1) (d) of the National Transportation Act, the act states:
Transportation is recognized as a key to regional economic development and commercial viability of transportation links.
Under this act it appears the National Transportation Authority can instruct CN to provide competitive and quality transportation to the Atlantic region.
I urge the Minister of Transport to bring the NTA into this urgent situation and act quickly to resolve this important issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ongoing difficulties the Canadian public and economy are having with the GST illustrates how out of step the government is with this country.
Last year the Prime Minister promised: "They're not going to pay a nickel more, not a nickel more" with the GST.
Yesterday The Financial Post announced: "Ottawa goofed on GST prices". The Toronto Star blamed the tax load for cross-border drain. And a survey conducted by the Consumers' Association of Canada found that close to 75 per cent of consumer items experienced a rise in cost thanks to the GST.
Moreover, revenue officials are reported to be stating that "the amount being collected by the GST far exceeds expectations". According to The Toronto Star "the GST collects billions of dollars more this year than the $24 billion expected".
Remember, the GST was supposed to replace only the MST revenue of $18.5 billion. But a 7 per cent GST on national goods and services valued at $410 billion annually will produce $28.7 billion, a full $10 billion more than the government claims.
Can the public be blamed for dismissing the Prime Minister's claims as nothing more than political puffery, totally divorced from reality?

Mr. Speaker, many allegations have been made that former Greek resistance fighters have used fraudulent documents to support their claims for the war veterans allowance.
I would like to acknowledge that action has been taken by our government in the following manner. As soon as the Minister of Veterans Affairs was informed that fraudulent documents might have been used by former Greek resistance fighters, the minister immediately asked the RCMP to conduct an investigation which is still under way.
In July 1990, when the RCMP provided proof that certain documentation was fraudulent, a new process was put in place to ensure that all new applications be verified by the Government of Greece. The department has also initiated a review of existing cases in pay.
To date, the Government of Greece has found a small number of applications to be fraudulent. In cases where these people have received money, the department has ceased payment and is acting to recover past payments.

Mr. Speaker, considering the government's undertaking in the last Speech from the Throne that it would review its policies in relation to the family, I would like to remind my government that improvements are urgently needed to correct the present situation. In fact, there are a number of major flaws in our taxation system.
Mr. Speaker, is it normal for a married couple with two children, where each spouse earns $17,500-a total family income of $35,000-to pay $852 more in income tax than a couple living common law, whose income and family situation are otherwise identical?
Is it normal to allow a married couple a deduction of $399 for a dependent child, when a couple that has decided to live common law can claim $5,141 for that child?
Is it normal for a man who is separated to be able to deduct from his income, as alimony paid to his exspouse, the total amount of living expenses of his dependent children, while the woman has to declare this as additional income on her income tax form?
Briefly, although the taxation system has evolved in terms of the changes that have taken place in the family structure over the years, the rules governing tax allowances have become inconsistent. The result is a system that is unwieldy, inefficient and unfair, and it should be reviewed and amended as soon as possible.

It is impossible to really discuss with a group of people who have
no authorized representatives.
Rather than pitting one group against the other and playing the politics and the game of "divide and conquer", when will the minister recognize that ultimately the federal government is the authorized and elected representative of these people who happen to be Canadians and who are legitimately demanding action, solution and leadership from this national government?
What is so wrong with that, Mr. Minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The hon. member from the other side may try to distort what I said to the people yesterday, but he certainly will not succeed in making the Canadian population believe that we have not met with the people involved. We have met with all the stakeholders in the trucking industry. I just came out of a meeting with the representatives of the Canadian Trucking Association.
So, we have met with all people and we have listened to them. On Friday we told the people assembled on the street that their concerns have been expressed by the Coalition of Independent Owner-Operators in the task force that we have created. This task force has asked for studies. These studies are coming forward and they will be wrapped up by the task force. Then we will address the problems based on facts and not on misconceptions.

The fact of the matter is that these truckers speak for more Canadians than this government's 14 per cent standing in the polls right now. That is the problem.
I ask the minister this: He said that he has met and talked with many people. He has had a nine-option plan proposed by this Liberal opposition party. He has had solutions from the truckers and their wives. He has had specific representations for over a year. I ask the minister, why is this government so reluctant to even usher in temporary relief measures?
May 22, 1991

Which will it be? Crossing every t and dotting every i of every study ever commissioned, or listening and responding to average Canadians and their plights?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy that the member has given me the occasion to respond and make known to the general public the Liberal way of meeting crises: Spend more money.
I have here a brochure put out this week by an hon. member. I want to quote one of his suggestions, and I would like everybody to listen to this: "7. Federal-provincial trade-off: Financial co-operation to ease the provincial tax portion on diesel fuel can be attained by the federal government agreeing to roll back its share of revenues supporting the road infrastructure".
Then there is an explanation, because that needs an explanation. He says: "The federal government presently contributes approximately 5 per cent of total highway expenditures in Canada. In the U.S., the federal government contributes 20 to 25 per cent. Our federal government"-listen to this-"should increase its share of contributions of total highway expenditures to 20 per cent". Quick-fix spending by the Liberals.

A year after the report of the task force on Barriers to Women in the Public Service, the same old attitudes keep women below the glass ceilings.
Today, the Public Service Commission reported that women working for the federal government resign at twice the rate of men. They fill most of the short-term positions, with no benefits, no security, no rights and they make only 55 cents for every $1 a man earns.
What does the minister have to say to the women of Canada about this abysmal treatment of women working for the Government of Canada?

Oral Questions
Our government, fortunately, has done much more than the Liberals did during decades of government. We have set very precise targets in each area to improve equity.
I fully agree that we need to continue to do more. We are doing that in every area. I remember, not so long ago, the Prime Minister giving numbers of achievements that we can be very proud of.
I can say that this government will continue to press with its effort. We have precise targets, and we are achieving them.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Targets require steps. Women make up nearly half the Public Service, but they got less than 25 per cent of management promotions last year, less than one quarter of the appointments to the management from outside the Public Service and just 20 per cent of the appointments within the management category.
One year ago, the former President of the Treasury Board said: "I can tell my colleague that the report is being acted on today. We are not going to hold up action on this report." When will the government give women more than empty promises?
When and how will this minister give women a chance at equality?

However, if you take for example the management categories when the Liberal Party, to which she belongs, was in power, there were 308 women in the management categories-that is, 7.3 per cent. We took power and today we have 730 women in management, or 15.3 per cent. We have more than doubled the number of women in the management categories and we will continue to move forward.

Clearly, because of the inflationary pressures and inflationary expectations which developed between 1988 and 1990, that issue had to be addressed or we would have ended up being in the same position that we were in 1981 and 1982 under the Liberals, where we had inflation rates of 13 per cent and 14 per cent and interest rates in excess of 20 per cent. We wanted to avoid that.
May 22, 1991

What has been indicated is that we have developed and put in place policies that will see us ease out of the recession in the second half. We expected the first half to be slow, but the economic indicators that we now see with respect to renewed business confidence, increased housing starts, increased housing sales and the decline in interest rates, we believe auger very well for recovery in the second half.

You left us cooling our heels for a while. But I wanted to follow up on what I heard the Speaker say and I hope that I heard him wrong. I heard him say that he is here to do what the majority of members want to be done.
Mr. Speaker, I really hope I heard wrong because, if indeed the Speaker of the House claims his role is to serve the majority, this means that, tomorrow morning, the majority could decide that there will be no question period and no speeches by opposition members, and the Speaker of the House would go along with that.
Mr. Speaker, I think this is a misconception of the role of the Speaker and all that time, as a minority member, I thought the Chair was here to protect me. I would like, Mr. Speaker, and I probably will, to reserve the right to raise a question of privilege because, if the Speaker has now decided to serve the majority, this institution is in grave danger. It is facing the threat of becoming undemocratic.
May 22, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I want the senior Speaker to realize that this is a statement that has to be clarified as soon as possible because I refuse to believe that the Speaker is only here to serve the majority.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, almost 125 years ago the first government of this nation was seized by a bold and a compelling dream.
The goal was to resist the unrelenting pull of the American states by stitching together a disparate group of northern colonies into the fabric of a nation. The government's vision was to bind the country together with ribbons of steel, providing the conduit for an entire nation's dreams, hopes and aspirations. And they did it.
New industry began to flow from one region to another, and ideas and dreams, packaged in letters, sped across thousands of miles. The railroad became the principal method for Canadians to share their goods, their culture and their need to communicate with one another.
Like most technologies, in time it was added to by faster, more efficient and cheaper methods. Railways were joined by aeroplanes, and rail cars by container trucks. The east-west bonds once again became susceptible to the tug of north-south industry and culture.
It was not just transportation that underwent this revolution; it was also communications.
In 1874, Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone in Brantford, Ontario. A former native of my own home town of Fergus, Reginald Aubrey Fessenden made the world's first radio broadcast of voice and music on Christmas Eve in 1906.
The Address
By 1990, the Canadian telephone industry was employing almost 100,000 workers and managing more than 35 billion phone calls each year, or nearly 1,400 calls for each and every Canadian. Telecommunications rapidly became the electronic railroad of today. Telephones and fax machines, robots and computers, electronic mail and desk top publishing are the methods Canadians use today to share their ideas, their dreams and their aspirations.
In that sense, telecommunications and cultural identity are absolutely dependent upon each other. Without communication, Canadians cannot develop shared values. Without the shared values which form the basis of our culture, we cannot define our Canadian identity.
I made these links because culture and communications are key to the three themes developed in the Speech from the Throne of unity, prosperity and a responsive government.
Under the theme of unity, the Speech from the Throne states that:
The ability of Canadians to live together in harmony and the ability of Canada to make a major contribution to world affairs depend upon our understanding of who we are as a people.
A changing world is challenging our values and severely testing our sense of self as a nation. Many of the old images which used to define how we see ourselves no longer hold the same relevance for Canadians today.
For example, how many of us sang The Maple Leaf Forever with its refrain of "thistle, shamrock, rose entwined''-which are the emblems of England, Ireland and Scotland-in school with the same reverence normally accorded the National Anthem? Yet today, more than 15 million Canadians claim a heritage which does not include either England, Ireland or Scotland. The thistle, shamrock and rose entwined is not, and some would argue never was, an image that fully represents Canada.
[Translation\
The challenge which confronts us, as the Speech from the Throne points out, is to "create a climate in which Canadians can deepen their understanding of their history and traditions and their appreciation of their country's rich diversity."

May 22, 1991
The Address
We deepen our understanding of history by visiting our museums. We learn more about our traditions by rediscovering our heritage. And we come to appreciate our diversity by being exposed to the cultural expression which thrives across this country.
In that sense, art and culture must be the key to this government's priority of building a unified and prosperous Canada. Discussions pertaining to our constitution are essential, as it is one element of what makes us Canadian. But it is also essential that we talk about the soul and spirit of the country.
In society, there are two broad ways in which we communicate. One is as a collective voice, be it through the speeches of our own elected officials, or the editorials of leading newspapers, or the way in which our media reflect our activities back to us.
But the other, and the more powerful, is the individual voice which speaks without censorship, without editing, without rewriting, without a committee dictating what can and cannot be said, and simply shouts out whatever can, and must, be heard from a personal point of view.

When our artists speak, whether on paper, on canvas or in clay, through the movement of their bodies or the flickering light on the cinema screen, they express our deepest thoughts. They see into the hearts of Canadians and focus bright light on what is real and what is true. Those countries in the world which have flourishing artistic communities inevitably also have a strong sense of identity. Regrettably, the men and women who dedicate their lives to their talent are not supported as generously in Canada as their talent deserves.
As the arts community knows so well, it has always been difficult for artists to earn enough to support their families. The average artist in Canada hopes to earn from $13,000 to $19,000 a year. These are particularly unimpressive figures when we consider that the average artist also has a university degree and at least 17 years of experience. Many are forced to take second jobs, thereby limiting the time they can devote to honing their skills. They live with recurring unemployment and fluctuating and sporadic incomes.
They do not fit the standard business relationship because their work is a labour of love. More than half of
the Canadian artists surveyed recently by Statistics Canada said that they considered their art a vocation rather than a business or a profession.
Because they fall through the cracks, qualifying over the course of their years neither as employees nor as employers, they have no professional status in our society and have limited recourse to the social safety net that the rest of us enjoy.
I had the good fortune almost seven years ago, when I was minister of revenue to work with the leaders of the arts community in Canada on the government's response to the report of the subcommittee on the taxation of visual and performing artists and writers. Together, we sat down and wrote new rules which recognized that artists play a unique role in Canada and that they deserve special consideration in tax administration. It was a good first step, but the time has come to take that principle further.
Our artists in Canada need a framework in law which acknowledges their special and distinctive contribution to our country and which allows them improved access to certain rights and benefits that other Canadians are privileged to enjoy.
This is not a new idea. The government and the arts community of Canada have recently completed years of intense collaboration, which has resulted in a bill on the status of the artist in Canada. It has been prepared in collaboration with the Canadian Conference of the Arts, with the performing artists' associations including AC-TRA, L'Union des artistes and Actors Equity, with creative artists and producers' associations, and with the Canadian Advisory Committee on the Status of the Artist.
This issue has been thoroughly reviewed by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture and the bill has been welcomed by our Prime Minister.
It provides recognition, unprecedented in federal law, of the professional status of our country's artists as well as their contribution to the development of our culture and our society.
It gives me great pleasure to confirm to the House that I intend to introduce this legislation on the status of the artist tomorrow. I am confident that all parties will recognize the value and the urgent need for this bill and agree to pass it as quickly as possible.
May 22, 1991

Improving the recognition received by Canada's artists is not a partisan issue. I will be seeking the support of my colleagues opposite in the hope that the bill can be sent to the Senate before we rise for our summer recess.
Each year the arts sector contributes billions of dollars to the economy and provides hundreds of thousands of jobs to Canadians, but the true value of the arts goes well beyond the economic. Their real value lies in their ability to civilize, to break down boundaries, to open up new horizons and to act as a mirror to our society.
The arts is an avenue beckoning us to discover who we really are as a people. And in helping us to understand who we are, the contribution of the arts to Canadian unity is both profound and enduring.
Just as art, culture and unity are intertwined, so are communications and prosperity, the second theme found in the Speech from the Throne.

Telecommunications is an essential building block to national prosperity, just as the railroad was a century ago.
Its chief value lies in its ability to act as an "enabler" to Canadians companies. Global telecommunications networks have made the flow of capital virtually instantaneous-transferring hundreds of billions of dollars daily among the world's major financial centres.
The markets of the world are now available to us with the bending of an elbow over the telephone, telex or fax machine.
But the telecommunications industry is also valuable in itself. Telecommunications is the premier high-tech industry in Canada today, one of only a few in which Canada is a world leader. It contributes 3.5 per cent of our GDP, or $21 billion a year-as much as agriculture, fisheries and forestery combined.
The opportunities for growth are substantial. The current world market for telecommunications equipment is estimated at beween $100 and $150 billion, of which Canada's share is but 4 per cent or $4 to $6 billion.
Our competitors are investing billions of dollars, which we cannot hope to match dollar for dollar. But we can strive to be more effective, to marshal our resources and
The Address
target them to the areas where they can do the most good.
However, as the Prime Minister stated in Vancouver last year, there is a third value to telecommunications. To borrow his words: "It would be hard to exaggerate the importance of the communications industry to Canada. It is a powerful instrument of economic and social development".
Telecommunications and its related technologies have the power to do tremendous social good by reducing the inequities we find between people. For example, the Department of Communications has been very active in improving the lives of disabled Canadians. We have developed a National Broadcast Reading Service for those who cannot read. We have closed captioning on TV for those who cannot hear. We have also developed special computerized telephones for those who have problems with speech.
Telecommunications also has the power to reduce inequities found in the regions. For example, in Newfoundland, we are using satellites to link the health care centres of 140 small, rural communities to help with emergency diagnosis and to provide training and upgrading.
In Manitoba, teachers felt their children were not getting enough attention in the maths and sciences. In response, working with the provincial government, we set up a Homework Hotline, which allows children to phone in questions to teachers in a television studio. The teachers answer the questions and their images are beamed by satellite into the cable systems so that students can watch them on television.
And, up north, we are helping to implement a native cultural and educational broadcasting network which will give northerners greater access to information and cultural programs.

Our technology makes it possible for us to meet our social responsibilities and to open up whole new worlds of information and learning to Canadians who might have no other access. It gives us the ability to respond to the needs of all Canadians-the third theme found in the Speech from the Throne.

May 22, 1991
The Address
Government responsiveness must play a large role in the future of telecommunications and culture in Canada. But our role must be fine-tuned to respond to the needs of today and tomorrow.
The days when governments could meet the needs of industry by simply handing over money are over. Our deficit is much too large and the competition much too sophisticated for that sort of an answer to work. If government is really to make a difference, it must concentrate on structural changes which will allow individuals and businesses to compete in new markets. The status of the artist legislation is a good example of a structural measure which governments can take to help Canadians help themselves.
A second example can be found in telecommunications. The industry is currently regulated by the Railway Act, 1904. It was a very good bill for the 19th century railroads, but it will not meet the needs of the 21st century telecommunications system. If we are to be competitive and effective, we will need a national, unified market. New legislation would help break down the barriers to trade between provinces, and I intend to discuss this issue with my colleagues both in government and in industry to see what can be done.
A third example can be found in the marketing and distribution of cultural products. In our enthusiasm to produce excellent products, we have sometimes forgotten to make sure that we have gained maximum access to the markets.
Larger audiences would go a long way toward ensuring growth in our cultural industries.
A few weeks ago, the Citizens' Forum on National Unity sent out a request to 2,000 visual artists living across Canada, asking them to send in works which expressed their feelings about this country. Last week, their entries were on display at the regional headquarters of the Ottawa-Carleton region. Some of the pieces were angry or critical, and that is fine. We were not looking for propaganda. We were looking for thoughtful expression. We were looking for people who were willing and able and talented enough to express what was deep inside.
There were two entries in particular which caught my attention. One, from Toronto, was a Canadian flag with a
fleur-de-lis and a maple leaf and a caption which read: "Keep building bridges", continuent a tisser des liens. The other, from Sydney, Nova Scotia, showed a Canadian flag with the maple leaf divided into 10 sections, one for each province, about to fall off to the side. Its caption was: "Unite or fall".
I was heartened by these entries because they expressed a sincere hope that Canada could resolve its problems and remain united. I think that is the way the vast majority of Canadians feel today.
As members of Parliament the demands on our time are many. We have no shortage of duties to fulfil. We have duties both in government and in opposition. We have duties to our constituencies, to our caucuses, to our parties, to our consciences. Whether we call ourselves Conservatives, Liberals or New Democrats, I believe that we agree our paramount duty is to the country that we love and cherish, the country which has allowed us to live in freedom, peace and prosperity.
Today that duty should speak to all of us. It tells us that we must discover the way to resolve the problems facing Canada, to rediscover who we are as a people, and to renew our appreciation of our history, our tradition and our rich diversity.
Most important, we must reject the claim by some that we can let our country slip away from us without enormous cost to every Canadian. We owe it to those who built this great country. We owe it to ourselves. And we owe it to our children.
May the Speech from the Throne, and this debate that follows, remind us of this most compelling of all duties.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to hear the minister in his first speech in the House on the Speech from the Throne and very pleased to hear his commitment to the well-being of artists and the general population with respect to culture.

If there is anything that defines a country internationally or globally it certainly is the culture that is left behind-what is written, what is painted, its stories, et cetera.
I think it is unfortunate-and I hope this minister will not be too unhappy in his task-that the previous three ministers were not as successful as I sincerely hope this minister will be.
The minister spoke about telecommunications, the size of that industry, the fact that it was an economic lever. We have all known that for quite some time, the fact that it is 3.5 per cent of our GNP or $21 billion. Yet since 1985 this government has been promising us a new and updated Telecommunications Act.
I wish this minister good luck, good health and long life. I hope he is able to introduce this bill. I would very much like to know what this minister is planning to do, as he spoke of the fact that it is through communications and cultural products that we have access to the world of art, the world of literature, and the world of people out there.
I would like to remind the minister that next week is access week for the disabled.
Is the minister aware of the fact that Braille books are produced by the CNIB and that we do nothing to enable the production of books in Braille? Is he aware of the fact that we have a tax on reading and a tax on literacy and that this is absolutely against any kind of principle found almost anywhere in the world? Does he realize that his predecessors brought in an incomplete copyright bill and that there should be copyright exemptions for books with large print to enable the poor-sighted to learn effectively and efficiently? In every other way they are normal but they have a problem with their sight.
Children and young adults in high school and college have their learning circumscribed because of the fact that this government has not been clear in its copyright legislation. It has not exempted the printing of such material from the laws of this land.
In terms of access I heard the minister talk about native programs. I suggest he go back and find out how much the past Secretary of State cut from those programs. He is now the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. Let him tell you what he did to native
The Address
programming in the north. Let the former minister tell you what was done about the satellite that was supposed to be provided so that there could be a proper distribution system up north.
We have a minister of good will and I would very much like to see him be successful in his task as it is in the best interest of national unity and the development of this country. He started off very well in his first speech to the constituency and everyone was very pleased to hear from him.
Last but not least I would like to know, before he tables his status of the artist legislation, which is very key to the well-being of the artist, if he recognizes the low income level of most artists in Canada. I believe it is around $12,000 a year, which is a nice starvation figure. If he does not address within that bill the kinds of tax measures that will make living viable so that artists can be productive, he is in effect window dressing and not looking at the real issues.
I ask the minister to do two things. First, tell the Americans that you are master of your own destiny as minister and bring in the film distribution bill in Canada. Second, for the artist and the creators, address the tax measures so that they are entitled to income averaging. If you know anything about the field of art and artists, you know that they have lean years and fat years, and they must be allowed to have income at-

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all thank my hon. colleague for her kind words and say how much I am looking forward to my new responsibilities in this portfolio. I will do my best to respond to the various points that she raised.

When it is complemented by other economic measures which are designed to improve the status of artists in Canada, I think it will begin to give to Canadian artists some recognition of the tremendous contribution they make to our national life. She asked that we serve notice on the Americans and on others of the fact that we in Canada want to have the ability to have our own unique culture. That was in essence the-

She mentions film distribution in particular, but in general the problem is one of ensuring that we have a unique voice in Canada and that it has the opportunity to be heard. Whether it is in films, book publishing, newspapers, radio, television, or a whole range of other areas, my goal is to ensure that Canadian voices are heard. My goal is not to prevent contact between Canada and the rest of the world. I think we are enriched by that contact. I do not believe that Canadian culture is frail and fragile and that it does not have something to offer the rest of the world.
Our voice to the rest of the world is strengthened and made more worth while to the extent that it is uniquely a Canadian voice. I have no hesitation in bringing in measures which help to protect the ability of Canadians to have their voices heard in Canada in a whole range of areas.

Mr. Speaker,
I would like to ask the minister if he would take a special interest-and I have written to him on this subject-in the whole question of media sensitivity and stereotyping, particularly as it applies to racial and ethnic minorities.
In particular, the Vancouver community is very, very concerned about a recent CBC series called The Dim Sum Diaries. There is not time to describe it, but I have written him about this. This is about the third time there have been programs-in this case on CBC, formerly on CTV and so on-that really stereotype a minority group.
I would like to ask the minister what he can do within his jurisdiction to try and encourage greater sensitivity in the media. Will the minister review CRTC policy and guidelines? Will the minister also take a look at how the Employment Equity Act and the multicultural bill itself is being applied within his jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to look into all the areas raised by my hon. friend. She raises in particular the issue of stereotyping and problems with a particular program on the CBC. I did notice in the newspapers that she had raised that issue on the west coast.
I know my hon. friend is as sensitive as I am to ensuring that governments do not reach into the CBC to instruct it as to what it can and cannot run in terms of specific programs. The principle of ensuring fair treatment, or the principle of ensuring that stereotyping does not take place, is a matter that is of concern to all members of Parliament. It is entirely legitimate for Canadians concerned about the content of any broadcast to raise those concerns with the broadcaster, with the minister who will convey those concerns to the broadcaster, and with the CRTC, where the regulator will try to ensure that licensees operate in an effective and fair way.
I could indicate also to my hon. friend an area that I bring with me from my old responsibilities of particular concern is that of image portrayed in the media particularly of women and children and the effect it might have on issues related to family violence.
When I was Minister of National Health and Welfare,
I asked that more be done to try to sensitize Canadians, particularly people within the media, to concerns about dehumanization of women and children, and portrayals of roles which could foster or could encourage violence in our society. This is certainly one of my concerns.
The issues she raised are all legitimate areas to be looked at.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this important occasion for the purpose of participating in the debate on the last week's Speech from the Throne. That speech was really a declaration of despair. It should have set new goals for our country and put in place a concrete plan of action to help Canadians climb out of the economic recession in which they now find themselves, an economic recession that this government brought on itself.
May 22, 1991

The Speech from the Throne offered no new hope and no new progress. This government has failed, and has failed Canadians once again. What unites my colleagues and me and gives urgency to our task is the need to define Canada's destiny and shape the society we all want. While the hopes of the Fathers of Confederation have become our record of Canadian accomplishment, it is the Liberal Party of Canada that has embodied the story of Canada's development for many decades.
For over 100 years, Liberals have sought to fulfil the aspirations of those Canadians seeking a better life and a better land. Traditional Liberal principles have given us purpose and direction, but we have also been innovative. We have responded to new concerns and new realities: from Alexander Mackenzie's political and electoral reforms in the 1870s to Pierre Trudeau's Charter of Rights and Freedoms a century later; from Wilfred Laurier's efforts toward self-government and foreign affairs to Mike Pearson's new Canadian flag and the Canada Pension Plan. This commitment to national progress has been a tenet of Canadian Liberalism when Liberalism was at its best. It developed railways, built the Trans-Canada Highway, the St. Lawrence seaway and the pipelines. The same commitment created a national airline, a major energy company and one of the world's best health care systems.
Our purpose and our progress was shaped by a faith and a power of hope over adversity. That purpose still lives. The Liberals did it and the leader of my party can and will do it again.
Progress has been our heritage; not that of the Conservatives or the NDP, and certainly not that of the Reform Party. The policies of the Mulroney government are policies that punish provinces and working people, deny education, destroy jobs and diminish opportunities. It is a government that presides over people who live on the edge of economic fear or who are experiencing the full and painful realization of those fears. Whether it is the savaging of rail passenger service, budget cuts at CBC or the tightening of purse strings for health care and higher education, the results are the same.
National institutions are being dismantled and destroyed. The destruction of Atlantic Canada is particu-
The Address
larly frustrating and sad to many of those Canadians who live in that region. Trains are gone, the planes are gone, our health care system is being threatened and the education of our young people could be limited. It is disheartening to see small towns filled with character, close families and unique identities slowly but consistently crumbling.
Rarely has a government in Canada been given such an historic opportunity to demonstrate vision and rarely has a government failed so badly.
Last week's Speech from the Throne and the budget that was brought down earlier this year completely failed to address the many problems and concerns all Canadians have and the hurt and the hardship that many Canadians must endure. The government had to prepare a budget and a throne speech in an economic situation produced by the cumulative effect of its own policies.
The size of the annual budget deficit since 1986-87 has not been reduced and the national debt has been about doubled in size. Unacceptably high interest rates and exchange rates have been maintained, producing a ma-de-in-Canada recession. Canada's competitiveness has further declined, bankruptcies have reached a record level, unemployment is rising and so is the tax burden and inflation.
The balance of payments in Canada's foreign indebtedness has seriously deteriorated and government revenues are falling.
This is the record of this government: a major recession, public finances out of control and the country itself in serious difficulties.
As recently as last September the former Minister of Finance declared before the Canadian Chamber of Commerce: "Our policy is working."
The minister was referring specifically to his monetary policy, which has caused the recession that all Canadians are now suffering through. One of the most remarkable features of the former Minister of Finance, in his tenure in office, is that over the years, in each and every budget speech, he maintained that his policies were working. His forecast of budget deficits, interest rates, growth rates and inflation rates have been consistently and repeatedly wrong time after time after time.

May 22, 1991
The Address
Another hallmark of the hon. member's career as Minister of Finance must surely be his aptitude at crafting a mythology instead of facing up to reality.
There are so many examples, but none more disturbing than the concluding words of the minister at second reading on the GST on January 29, 1990, when he said:
I believe that in the months following January 1,1991, when the cut and thrust of partisan debate on this issue has calmed down, when the controversy has subsided, when Canadians can see our economy even more vibrant and growing, they will conclude, as I have, that this is the right policy for the right reasons at the right time.
We are now in the months following January 1, 1991, and if our economy is now "even more vibrant and growing", it is only I suggest in the minister's mind. It is because the former Minister of Finance was more interested in crafting the myth than dealing with reality that he and his government must bear the full responsibility for Canada's current financial and economic situation.
Perhaps we should talk to the truckers, those many men and women who are losing their jobs and their homes. They see no solution to their tragedy but to come to the front steps of the House of Commons and plead for help from the Minister of Transport.
Perhaps this Minister of Finance should speak with senior citizens, perhaps he ought to speak to students and single parents across this country, those Canadians who are among the least able to pay more in tax and those Canadians who are suffering so unfairly. These are the Canadians on whom the burden of the Mulroney government's new taxes have fallen and will fall again.
This government must stop attacking the middle class and the working poor, those many Canadians in every province and territory who get by each day on nothing more than pennies and yes, prayers. This government has raised the taxes on working Canadians 31 times since 1984. In fact, income tax revenues collected by this government have increased by 70 per cent since the Conservative government was elected in 1984 with most of the increases being taken from middle-class families.
This government has doubled the national debt and has in fact piled up more debt than all of Canada's Prime
Ministers since Sir John A. Macdonald. In this government, tax reforms have had the result of raising personal income taxes by replacing deductions with tax credits, by deindexing tax brackets and by introducing the so-called clawbacks of social welfare legislation such as family allowance and old age pensions.
Our goal must be a simpler and fairer tax system. The Conservative government has tried and has failed. As well, the incomes of middle-class families have not kept ahead of inflation since this government was elected and these families are finding themselves increasingly in debt as they struggle to attain the goals of a middle-class life; a home, a college education for their children and a comfortable retirement.
These are hard times for these honest people. The tax policies that favour the few and punish the middle class are unacceptable to my party and I believe they are unacceptable to Canadians across this country.
There are many ways to raise money or to save money than to increase an already unfair tax burden. We do not accept the belief that savings in federal spending can be achieved only by eliminating or devastating programs that help the poor, the elderly, the ill, the young and the disadvantaged.
Even the minister's seventh and last budget was an economic failure. In point of fact, this budget has been characterized by one of Canada's leading financial institutions, none other than the Toronto-Dominion Bank and I quote: "It is probably the most economically inept and destructive budget since 1930s". These are strong words, but words that are warranted when the record is examined.
The 1991 budget papers' treatment of the recent economic performance is particularly damning. It confirms that the retrenchment in interest, sensitive consumer demand, cuts in business investment and manufacturing decline, all signs of an impending'recession were evident at the time of the 1990 budget. A year ago, there was an unmistakable set of warnings about the trouble the Canadian economy was heading for. The then Minister of Finance had an opportunity to change course and stop pursuing policies which were driving the country into a recession. But, no, he stuck to that policy.
May 22, 1991

Even more surprising, in 1990 the minister continued to daydream in spite of the harsh reality depicted in his own budget papers. Once again he expressed confidence that after a short economic slowdown in the first half of 1990, the imbalances would be corrected, mostly by natural forces in the economy and sound non-inflation-aiy growth would be resumed in 1991.
Last year the minister's predictions were regarded by most economic observers as totally unrealistic. The reality is that the macroeconomic policies pursued by the Minister of Finance did not work and they have produced this recession. The government has also failed to deal responsibly with big budget deficits.
Those with long memories will recall how the Minister of Finance described his strategy for controlling the national debt in his first budget of May 1985. He called it the: "clear and realistic medium-term plan". Those were the buzzwords.
Last year, that is five years after the plan was launched, the minister was still referring to it in his budget, in spite of the consistent failure of his plan to reduce the deficit. The record speaks for itself.
The cost, however, paid by all Canadians for these and the minister's other mistakes have been a dramatic increase in the tax burden, particularly upon individuals. Sadly, Canada has joined the ranks of the most internationally indebted countries and our future ability to manage monetary policy will be even more restrained in the future.
For all these reasons the former Minister of Finance and this government will be judged severely, not only for their poor or indifferent economic management, but for the gross lack of vision when we faced the greatest current challenge to Canada's existence as a dynamic and a united country.
The clear and realistic plan of budget deficit reduction has failed. The economic renewal plan has failed and the five-year plan for further deficit reduction is in the course of failing.
Nowhere is the Tory record of failure more evident that in my own province of Nova Scotia. The Atlantic Provinces Economic Council predicts that real growth in my province will be limited, with almost no growth at all in the economy. In Cape Breton, unemployment is running at about 20 per cent or double the national average where statistics can be found. Many stores and
The Address
restaurants in the Sydney and Glace Bay area have closed their doors. Jobs are disappearing and hope of finding another one does not exist any more.
Hotels and restaurant operators in Cape Breton say that the number of bus tours fell by as much as 14 per cent last year, with American tourists complaining about high prices and high taxes. American tourists, like so many Canadians, do not like the Prime Minister picking their pockets every time they go to a local shopping mall, see a movie, go out to dinner with their family or visit the comer store.
Times continue to be tough in fishing towns such as Lockeport and Digby, where the fish processing plants closed and put a town out of work. And now in my own small town of Louisbourg, signs are evident that real danger is on the horizon.
Halifax, the capital of our province has its problems too. The Metro Food Bank is feeding more than 7,000 people a month, 40 per cent more people than it did in
1989.
There are many things one could refer to with regard to the throne speech. But let it be said that this is a very, very difficult time for this country both economically and politically.
I believe that young Canadians want their leaders to exercise prudent judgment on their behalf, not only for the short term but certainly for the long term as well.
The essential question facing our country has always been the reconciliation of Quebec nationalism with Canadian nationalism. While we can point with pride to our past, Confederation's agenda remains unfinished. Quebec and its people must become a full partner in our national life. Greater efforts must be taken to ensure that that occurs. Whatever the differences between English Canadians and French Canadians, it is vital that French Canadians be assured of the future of their language and culture.
Beyond these concerns, we must work to strengthen the common ties that bind together, ties of history and of kinship. Whatever the differences between Quebec and the rest of Canada, they must be overcome because the relationship between English Canadians and French Canadians is essential to the nation at the present time. More, it is critical to our own future and to the very meaning of our Canadian way of life.

May 22, 1991
The Address
Surely the hope of this nation lies in the acceptance of our differences, our distinctiveness and the recognition of our common problems and our common purpose. That is what John A. Macdonald and George Cartier had in mind in Charlottetown in 1864, when beneath the old gas lamps in the old Prince Edward Island legislature, they committed themselves to building a new nation with a new Constitution.
Today, that same challenge faces us anew. Today, more than ever, Canadians need a vision of what their country can become. We can choose, as parliamentarians, between industrial vitality or industrial decline, between national renewal or national ruin.
If we do not try to change things today, we may not have a chance tomorrow. We must demand a fair deal for families and a fighting chance for our young people. To be involved in that effort is to be involved with the same spirit that fired the imagination and efforts of the first settlers to New France several centuries ago.
In closing, every one of us can be a pioneer in our own time, blazing by thought and service a trail to a better and brighter future. Together, my colleagues and I on this side, are determined to carry our great democratic experiments proudly forward; rekindle the commitment to the human spirit on which the greatness of our country depends; and yes, to pledge our future to building a better Canada in every region, province and community across this great country.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the observations and the question of the hon. member opposite. I am not prepared to apologize to the hon. member for the picture I had painted for her in terms of what is out there across this country. The hon. member must realize that, notwithstanding the fact that she is a member of the government and enjoys a majority at this point in time, there are many, many Canadians who are in deep economic anguish. However, the hon. member asked for my answer and I will respond if she would just be a little bit courteous and listen to my response regarding her observation. There are many Canadians who suffer great, great economic anguish, who are greatly concerned about what is taking place politically in this country in terms of national unity.
I do not make apologies for standing up on behalf of those truckers outside. I make no apologies for standing up for the unemployed in my constituency. I make no apologies for standing up for those individuals, both young and middle-aged, who want a fair shake from government and have been denied it. I make no apology whatsoever for putting on the record that there are thousands upon thousands of Canadians whose economic plight has been driven into the ground, down through the ground, by the policies of the government opposite.
May 22, 1991

The hon. member has posed a very specific question: What is my blueprint? I will give the hon. member just a little sample.
The other day we had an opposition day where we put forward a motion regarding the trucking industry. The transport critic for our party laid on the table nine specific points that the government could pursue without great cost, many of them without great cost to the taxpayers, either provincially or federally. All the government did was thumb its nose at them.
That is one point I want to bring to the hon. member's attention.
Second, the hon. member talks about the blueprint. One of the essential ingredients of an economic blueprint has to be monetary policy. The monetary policies of this government, in terms of its high dollar and high interest rates, are choking small and medium-sized businesses across this country. It is preventing companies from going out and hiring individuals they would normally want to hire.
I believe, as I am sure the hon. member believes, very much in the private sector. We have to facilitate the private sector, which is the engine of growth in this country. That certainly cannot be done with a monetary policy which chokes small business and medium-sized business. You don't do that. That is what this government has done in the regions of this country, in my own region of Atlantic Canada.
It is absolutely devastating. I am not joyful about standing on the floor of the House of Commons and telling members of the plight of those Canadians, but that is the responsibility that I have as a member of Parliament.
The member can speak from her seat and say: "your specific plan". There are three items that the member could act upon. However, the member won't act upon it, just as the member failed to act with regard to what Canadians were saying on the GST and a host of other things.
The hon. member knows very well the answers, the courses of action that have led to this economic recession. The government refuses at every opportunity to accept cogent, prudent advice and change its ways.

We hoped that with a new Minister of Finance we may see some light at the end of the tunnel, but unfortunately he is sticking to those old policies.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to add a few of my thoughts and words to this debate on the throne speech. By their nature, speeches from the throne are usually pretty general. Other speakers and media commentators have pointed out that they tend to lack specifics. They are not unlike a motto though, something that sets a tone and a direction.
Before being elected to this place, while serving as mayor, I wrote a motto for my municipality. We said that we had pride in our past and faith in our future.
That same motto should apply to our country today. The Royal Canadian Legion borrowed our motto for its diamond anniversary celebration. I am proud to share anything with the Royal Canadian Legion. I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to compliment the Dominion Command of the Legion for its recent initiative on national unity.
There is no group in Canada that has more invested in this country than do its members. The men and women who stood strong to defend our way of life are now, through their national unity campaign, continuing to
fight to preserve the country in which they have invested so much.
I believe in the Canada they have worked for. I am very proud of our history.
In reflecting on that motto, one of the reasons that Canadians today may look to the future with discouragement is that they have not learned enough of our past. They do not have the pride in our Canadian history that they should have. Ours is a history of strong people who were willing to put aside individual differences and build a nation, a nation that exists today and is the envy of much of the world.
As members of Parliament, we have all had the opportunity to attend citizenship court. The most recent one I attended in Red Deer had 34 people from 18 different countries. Every one of them was there, not to become a hyphenated Canadian, but to become a Canadian.
In discussing with them afterwards, a number expressed amazement at how little Canadians knew about their own history. There is an old saying that if you do not appreciate what you have, you are going to lose it.
During the recess we each had the opportunity to spend some extra time with our electorate. We must have all heard that which we know, that we face serious challenges in our country and we are at a turning point in Canadian history.
There is a great malaise across this nation of ours. Canadians are concerned. They are also frustrated and upset. It is my strong personal opinion that we must be open to discussions on change in this very institution. However, the throne speech points out many other areas of change that Canadians must be open and receptive to.
There are many agendas across the nation and each is important to the people in those areas, and indeed to Canada as a whole. In my own province we want to see the Senate made responsive to the needs of Canadians and capable of defending the rights of the provinces. It is time for a major change.
I appreciated the comments of the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs when he said that Senate reform would be one of the items that he would be addressing.
May 22, 1991

Challenges present opportunities and I see a major opportunity given us right now. The ongoing discussion, indeed the conflict and the questions have Canadians involved and attentive to the happenings in this House. The level of involvement and concern possibly makes politicians uncomfortable, but I think that is healthy. People should be aware of what goes on in their political institutions, and those of us who serve in political office have to be ready to accept comment and constructive criticism.
The economy and our ability to compete internationally is another reason why we must work together. A diminished Canada would diminish each of the regions as well. Those who believe otherwise are fooling themselves. It is true that in an individual sense the day-today activities of our lives might not be affected. We would still live in the same house, drive the same car, shop in the same store. The sun would still shine, the rain still fall and the seasons pass, but Canada would be diminished and there would be an economic price paid by all. We would lose our place at the G-7, our international prestige would diminish, and the resulting uncertainty could tie up courts and political effort for years. International monetary markets would question investment in this country. None of us can afford that uncertainty, and no thinking Canadian wants it.
Executives at major Canadian corporations were quoted in the press last week as saying:
The separation of Quebec would do more than divide Canada. It would eliminate jobs and send investment, plants and opportunities to the United States, Europe and Asia.
It went on to say that our unity is strengthened by a strong economy and prosperity is enhanced by a united country, but that disunity in the face of global economic challenge invites decline.
I love this country. Canada is a great nation. I believe it became the great nation it is because of the core values it was developed upon: the belief in God and the dignity and worth of the individual.
Our society was built on the foundation of faith, family and community. I was encouraged by the one sentence in the throne speech where His Excellency said:
My government will review its policy in relation to the family, the most fundamental building block of Canadian society.
There is systemic discrimination against the traditional family. It is wrong when a single parent will question
The Address
whether he or she will get married because of the income tax implications and the child tax credit. It is wrong that two senior citizens would question whether to marry because of pension implications.
One sentence in the throne speech is not much, but I will be joining other members of our caucus in this House to encourage the government to act on it.
In many areas of the world the conflicts that exist within Canada today would be the basis of armed conflict. The hon. member for Edmonton Southwest recently remarked that we are engaged perhaps in a form of civil war in Canada, only in typical Canadian fashion we are trying to talk ourselves to death. We have problems and we are talking, and I believe we have the resolve to address them and to work out amiable solutions.
I feel it is very important that we try to understand and get to know people in all regions of Canada.
Recently the hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs told rural Albertans that he and his family still live on the same land that was farmed by his father, grandfather, great-grandfather, back 11 generations. Nobody loves the land like an Alberta farmer, and to think of one family inhabiting one piece of land for 325 years gave them cause for serious thought.
Last summer I had the occasion to attend a special anniversary for the McAllister family in the Antler Hill district. It was celebrating the 100th anniversary of the arrival of the first McAllister to farm that land. This year, I plan to join the residents of Willowdale as they too celebrate the centennial of their rural community. These people are proud of their land and they are proud of their heritage. Their forefathers rode across Canada by wagon, by horse and by train to come to an unknown and uncertain part of this country. By coming to the west they helped to build a nation. We, their descendants, are very proud today of what they built. We are proud to be Albertans, but above all, we are proud Canadians and we know that any reduction to Canada is a reduction to us all.
In closing, I have a short poem to which I am sorry I cannot ascribe any author. I have checked it and it is listed as anonymous.

May 22, 1991
The Address
I stopped to watch them tear a building down Some working men in my hometown.
With a heave and ho and a yes, yes yell,
They swung a beam and a sidewall fell.
I asked the foreman,'Are these men skilled?
The type you'd hire if you were to build?"
He chuckled and said, "No, indeed.
The commerce of labour is all I need.
For I can destroy in a day or two
What skilled men worked many years to build".
And I thought to myself as I wandered away Which of these roles do I plan to play.
During our constitutional discussions and during the debate, there are all too many people in this country who have been willing to play the role of the destructor; the person who is willing to sit back, criticize and tear down the efforts of the others who are trying to build. We are the recipients of the efforts of many men and women who have constructively worked together in a struggle to forge a consensus and who have toiled with their minds and their bodies to develop the land, a land that is the envy of the entire world and a country that sits as an example.
I am confident that we can ignore the naysayers and overlook those who would simply criticize and tear down for their own political or personal reasons, because the needs of Canada are greater than the needs of any individual. Canada is worth fighting for. Should we succeed in our efforts to overcome the many problems and challenges that face us today, history may record this period as nothing more than a footnote. Should we fail, we will have to explain to our children and grandchildren what we were doing when Canada was ripped apart.
I was elected as an Albertan. I was also elected as a Canadian. I was not elected to see this country torn apart and I want my efforts to be recorded on the side of those who are willing to work and add my skills to the building of the greatest nation in the world, my Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to reply to the question of the hon. member for Vancouver East. It is not often that those of us who inhabit the backbenches get their name in Quorum and not too often do we get a chance to explain.
As the member well knows, each one of us in this House is very often interviewed by people from the media. They take our comments and they write them up. Quite often they attach their own headings and they editorialize a little bit in the comments.
The comments in Quorum today attributed to me were part of an extremely long interview that I did with one of my weekly newspapers. It took about a page and a half of the paper to do the whole thing. There were certain elements taken out of it and recorded, one of which was my comments on multiculturalism.
I touched on this very briefly in my comments when I referred to the citizenship court. Canada is made up of different ethnic groups, and Alberta is a tremendous example. In that diversity there is strength. It is also beautiful that we have so many cultures come together. I personally encourage those people to pay attention to their heritage because we have to know our heritage. If we do not appreciate our heritage, we do not appreciate what we have in the present and we cannot plan for the future.
At the same time, there has been no period in Canadian history when we needed to develop a sense of being Canadian more. My comments were critical of any funds that went to a hyphenated Canadian group. I do not feel that we should be encouraging people to stress their differences. Encourage them to recognize their own heritage, by all means, as that is important, it is the strength of Canada, but my comment was that the Government of Canada should not be funding people to be hyphenated Canadians. It is important at this juncture of our history that we develop a sense of community, being together, and what makes us the same, not what makes us different.
May 22, 1991

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 1, Canada will be 125 years old. It is going to be an uneasy birthday because we are wondering if we are going to reach 126, and if we do, what kind of Canada we will have. Will we have a unified Canada, a divided Canada or a Balkanized Canada? Those are the questions that are going through all of our minds and we are very worried about our country.
I mention that because there seems to be a mood in this House that has not been evident in past years: we do want a strong Canada, a united Canada. We have to work a little bit harder to ensure that happens, especially as we approach Canada's 125th birthday. We are only a month and a half away and I think that thought is really bearing pretty heavily on our minds.
Just to emphasize this, last evening I was leaving the House of Commons with a Liberal member of Parliament from the Moncton riding. He had with him a couple of relatives. Their names were Georgie and Murray Seeley from London, Ontario. They wanted to talk about Canada, and we talked very freely.
One of the things that Mrs. Seeley pointed out to me was that she and her husband, who are both World War II veterans, are very worried about what might be happening. Her question to me was: "Do you think we will get through this thing?" That seems to be the dominant question, the theme that is on everyone's mind.
That generation seems to have more of a feeling for this country than maybe the rest of us, because it knows what it is like to have to work for something and to preserve something worth preserving.
In the course of that conversation she asked about one of my. constituents, whose name is Lome Groom. They served together during that war and when Mr. and Mrs. Seeley mentioned the relationship with Mr. Groom, it brought back a lot of memories.
The Address
I mention this again for a very specific reason: to point out the sacrifices that many Canadians have made for our country.
Lome Groom was a very young man in World War II. He is a double amputee who worked very hard and went through university. He raised a fabulous family and still resides in St. Stephen. In fact last week he experienced a great hardship when his wife passed on very unexpectedly-
When we look at people like the Seeleys, the Grooms and others around this country who have sacrificed so much, it really explains in toto why they are so nervous and upset with what is happening. They want to see us confident that we are going to get through this thing.
To me, the mood in this House is that we want to work together to ensure that we do get through our difficulties. We do want a united and strong Canada. We have to work to make it happen. We have taken so much for granted in this country in the last 25 or 30 years. Maybe it has been too easy for us. Maybe it is time that we reflect on the past and the sacrifices that Canadians, who in many cases are older than us, have made for the country and why they are so worried about it.
Despite all the difficulties that we are going through, we tend as Canadians to ignore the positive. There is so much happening in this country that is positive.
I am going to quote from a speech the Prime Minister gave in Calgary on April 22 of this year: "Those who claim that Canada's standard of living and quality of life, our social safety net and our legal system, our culture and our international status add up to failure must have a very strange definition of success. The evidence proves the contrary". The Prime Minister went on to point out that we could not afford to be complacent in this country.
But we are successful. Do we throw that success down the drain? Do we throw it all away? No, we do not. Canadians do not want to throw it all away. We simply have to work harder to continue the kind of success that Canada has enjoyed in the past number of years.

May 22, 1991
The Address
In terms of economic strength Canada is number eight in the world, although in terms of population we rank 31st. We have earned our place and we have to maintain it. We have earned our place at the economic summit. We sit beside countries like the United States, Japan, France, United Kingdom and Italy. We have earned our place. We have to maintain it, but we are not going to do it by being complacent. We have to get at the reasons why we were successful in the past. We have to respond to changes that have to come about but which are not always easy.
We have to take a very strong look at our educational system in this country and what we are doing. Some of the alarming statistics point out that we are not doing it all right. It is estimated that 40 per cent of new jobs created by the year 2000 will be highly skilled. Today, that figure is only 24 per cent.
One of the things that we are very conscious of is that at 30 per cent Canada has one of the highest high school dropout rates in the world. It is 30 per cent. As a nation we spend more on education than 90 per cent of all other countries in the world.
Yet, we have statistics that are so alarming. They point out that a large percentage of our population is not functionally literate. Given those alarming statistics, do we have any hope of competing in the future? Do we have any hope of competing against countries in the world that are changing or have changed with the times, that are willing to commit and have committed resources to those changes that are being dictated to us? We cannot go on in the old sense of doing things, the old ways of doing things.
The Speech from the Throne simply indicates that Canada and this government are willing to move with the times and make the changes that are necessary to ensure that future Canadian generations will be as prosperous as we have been in the past. We are going to commit the resources to ensure that happens.
When Canadians look at us and scrutinize us very carefully in this House in the coming weeks, I hope they can identify that sense of urgency, that we realize what has to be done and we are going to work together to make it happen. A unified Canada is a prosperous Canada. We need to have that economic prosperity, that dedication to task, to make it happen. I am convinced that we will and it will not be the politicians who do it. It will be Canadians themselves who will do it.
The cynicism that surrounds politicians is very understandable. From time to time in this House Canadians
witness unnecessary heckling and criticism back and forth across the floor and they wonder what we are doing here to resolve some of the difficulties.
I think the urgency of the times has drawn a line across that type of behaviour and we realize we have to work together. We can have our differences, but we are going to have to work very hard to get through this thing.
On July 1, when we celebrate our 125th year, maybe we will have that sense of optimism that we are going to make it to 126. We are only going to do it by working together, working for that common goal which is a prosperous Canada, a unified Canada.

I want to comment on the lack of concrete plans in the Speech from the Throne for jobs for Canadians at the present time. I have a question that I want to ask the hon. member.
I know that in my own province of Prince Edward Island the unemployment rate is running roughly 2 per cent more than it was at this time last year. We have a lot of people looking for jobs, as we have all across this country.
We look to this Speech from the Throne to offer them some hope, and here again the government has let them down. Not only that, but last week in my province we were told that the GST centre which was to open in the fall of 1992 will now be delayed one year until 1993.
When the Prime Minister promised this, he said it would be open in the fall of 1992. Then it was delayed until January 1993, then to June 1993, and now we are into the fall of 1993.1 must say that last weekend I had a number of people speak to me who were beginning to doubt the commitment of this government to ever open that centre.
I have never heard a logical reason for this delay. It has been reported in the press that some government officials have said that the delay has to do with the battle that this party, my party, waged against the GST. That is absolutely foolish. I want to ask the hon. member: Does he agree that the lack of job creation possibilities in the Speech from the Throne, coupled with delays like the GST centre in Summerside, are completely unacceptable?

Mr. Speaker, in direct answer to the question regarding the GST centre, that would probably be more appropriate if it were answered by the minister in the House. I am sure the hon. member will put that question to the appropriate minister soon, if she has not already done so.
With regard to the big picture of the economy, one of the things that the opposition fails to recognize is that Canada is part of the western world. The decline in the economy, and if you want, to a recession in the western world, is something that we cannot avoid because we are international players, international traders, and we cannot escape that reality.
If the member would look beyond just Canada, and I know that she does, the devastation in the U.S. with regard to the slowdown in its economy, has been greater than it has been in Canada, far greater. That does not remove us from our own responsibilities. In that sense we have a tremendous responsibility, no question about it, to get the economy moving again.
I believe that we will because I believe that the policies we are putting forward are the types of policies that will get us through the hard times and will create a stronger and more vibrant Canadian economy.
We cannot remove ourselves from the real world. We cannot buy our way out of problems. That was the tendency of previous governments.
Mr. Speaker, if you give me just a minute, I want to explain this. This pen-I often do this when I am speaking to groups-I pull it out of my pocket and I say, this has been the biggest enemy of the Canadian taxpayer since Confederation, especially the last 25 or 30 years. For the last 25 or 30 years successive governments and politicians from all sides-I am not just picking on the Liberals or the NDP, I can say it about Conservative

governments as well-have pulled this pen out of their pockets and just written the cheque, knowing dam right well the money was not there. What did we do? We saddled the Canadian people with a huge debt because the easy answer for those 25 or 30 years was write the cheque, buy off the Canadian people. What we were doing was mortgaging the country.
I do not want to see that happen. It will not happen with this government. It did not happen in the last budget brought forward by this government and it is certainly not reflected-
