speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that some people in this House realize that this is probably one of the most important debates so far as a throne speech is concerned that we are going to have because it will be during this session that many of the national problems concerning the national unity of this nation will have to be grappled with and, indeed, solved.
Therefore, we must take a very serious approach to this whole business of national unity and the economy. I am a firm believer that when people are dissatisfied over the economy, it certainly gives them more to complain about what is happening in the country. It is weakening national unity at the same time.
In previous speeches in the House, I have said that what this good old nation of Canada needs is a good dose of healthy national spirit. I do not think we are going to get this if we are going to keep on complaining inwardly about ourselves and if we are going to be downgrading ourselves in the eyes of the world.
We have indeed been given a great nation to manage. What we have to do is talk more about our opportunities in this country. We have to talk about the assets that we have been given, that we have inherited in this nation. We have to talk about what the Fathers of Confederation set going-and not just the Fathers of Confederation, but those people before them who for years built the colony which eventually became the nation.

May 22, 1991
The Address
The Fathers of Confederation had great insight for people in that particular age. Many things have happened to date that they could not visualize any more than we in this House today or anyone across this nation is going to visualize what is going to happen in the next 25 years of Canadian history. The country will have to adjust accordingly. We may well have to adjust our Constitution along the way to meet those challenges.
I think we, as Canadians, have to realize that God has given us a great land. We have indeed been blessed. If we do not manage it correctly, then we have no one to blame but ourselves. But there must be the right attitude. You cannot do it if you have a lot of negative attitudes. If you do not have a positive attitude, you are not going to build anything.
We in this nation have seldom been without the necessities of life. Indeed, there have been some people across the country who have experienced hard times and who have had difficult moments in their lives looking after their families, but we have found that for Canadians generally, be it at the community level or be it with our social programs in Canada, a great deal has been done to help everybody over those rough periods here in this nation of ours. We must never lose that feeling of empathy, that feeling of concern for our fellow individuals, any more than we should lose that feeling of empathy and concern for the international community. No nation in the world has been able to build the international highways of good will that have been built up by former statesmen in this House, former public servants in Canada and former Canadians generally.
It is indeed a great time. People say: "Oh, they are challenging times, things are difficult, my goodness what are we going to do next?" Well, what we do is sit down and get going on the challenge. You don't sit around wringing your hands, complaining and bickering and badgering.
I want to mention the economy one more time at the beginning of my speech. During modem day times when the economy goes flat, it affects far more Canadians than it ever did before. Even during the "dirty thirties", as people called them, by far the largest portion of Canadians still lived on farms and in small rural communities, were able to plant a garden and grow potatoes and kill the pigs in the fall, and they got by. They got by, but why? What added quality was there?
They got by because those Canadians, in many cases our parents, came through that because they had a faith. That is something that we have got to develop, within our own minds and our own mentality today. Do we have a faith to go ahead and build this nation? Do we have a faith to go ahead and work hard and be productive? Do we have a faith to believe in Canada?
I don't say this by way of criticism, Mr. Speaker, but I have heard people get up in this House and say: "I am an Albertan", "I am a Quebecer", "I am so-and-so". Well, Mr. Speaker, I am a Canadian. I may live in Ontario, and I am proud to live in Ontario and to have grown up there, but as a federal member of Parliament, I am a Canadian. If we are going to start building a national spirit in this country, we have got to forget those former terminologies that describe us, and from day one we are Canadians. We must make up our minds that we are going to build a national spirit in this country that will give great pride to Canadians at large.
Leadership is very important. Every time we get up in this House and start talking the blues and bickering and bantering with one another, we are discouraging Canadians. We have to stand up in this House and say first of all that we need to have faith in ourselves and we need to have faith in our fellow members in this House and in the other chamber. We have to realize that we are here to do a job for the people of Canada. We have to realize that we are here as federalists and that we are going to build a nation that we are going to be proud of.
We are very vocal at times in criticising the Americans and the way they build up their country and their pride and so on. We sometimes look upon that as being a bit artificial, but when the President of the United States gets on national television and asks the American people to pull together for the good of the nation, they do it. We must have a strong base where we, ourselves, have faith in this nation, where we implant that faith in all Canadians.
People came here from other countries and are Canadians today. They have adopted this country. Some of them have greater faith in this nation than we have demonstrated. I think that is a shame. Let us begin with that premise.
May 22, 1991

The other thing that sometimes bothers me in this House is comments about politicians. Yes, we know. I have been around long enough to know when people are angry and when they are in good humour. That is a cycle in politics. There are difficult times. A certain generation of politicians may start arguing and bickering at one another and give people the wrong impression. People blame it on television in the House, but there were wars on the floor of this House of Commons long before television was ever heard of. People ask me: "Does television make a difference?" Television makes a difference, but people across Canada see what is going on here.
However, if we would have had television in this House in 1917 when we had the great debate on conscription across this country, people would not have thought too much of politicians at that time either. This is not a new phenomenon, but it does mean that we have to clean up our act. There is nothing wrong with having strong debates, that is the name of the game. This House is not going to become a puritanical temple where people are not going to argue with one another in honest and earnest debate from time to time. There will always be very strong debate in this House.
Politicians sometimes downgrade themselves by admitting that they are not really showing a good image of themselves, that the people are angry with them because they are not doing their job properly or because they are debating. The first thing we have to realize is that this is a debating institution. From there on, as far as behaviour is concerned, it comes down to the question: "Do we have faith in ourselves and do we have faith enough to have earnest debate back and forth across the floor of this House without getting nasty?"
There is a good old rule in politics that I always use, and in my experience it normally works. If you treat the average individual with a little sense of decency and common sense, they will respond twofold. If we, once in a while, gave them a little encouragement verbally in this House, that would do a great deal to encourage them to go ahead with their daily jobs.
Do not downgrade ourselves as politicians. I am proud to be an elected member of this House of Commons. I am proud to be an elected Canadian who can get up and speak on behalf of my constituents, and even for the larger community abroad from coast to coast to coast in
The Address
this nation. We must realize the great assets we have, the great things we have to work for. We must take examples from those who came to this country with nothing and have succeeded. That is what we have to do. We are only going to do it if we have the energy and determination to do it ourselves.
I want to discuss regional development factors. If we are going to develop a Canadian nation, it has always been the case, over the decades of Canadian history, that as regional development goes, so goes the nation.
Northern and eastern Ontario are in a downturn now. What is happening in Toronto? Toronto is in a downturn because it is losing industry. The larger urban centres of our nation suffer when the regions that feed them suffer because they do not get the same input and do not have people doing the same kind of business with them from right across that particular region.
These are basic economic issues for the future development of Canada. What are important issues in regional development? Well, it has to be admitted that the free trade agreement, regardless of what we think of it on either side of this House, has hurt agriculture in this country. There is no question about that.
The dairy industry is very concerned and has been for some time. There is no question whatsoever that the famous memorandum of understanding, signed by a former Minister of International Trade who now has the delight of sitting in the Senate as a reward, putting a 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber to the United States hurt the lumber industry. We in northern and eastern Ontario, and in particular this region, have seen the effects of that since day one. There is no question about it.
When we see 300 people walking away from a sawmill, we think of the 15 per cent export tax, we think of high interest rates and an artificially high Canadian dollar. Then we think of all the added expenses the truckers have to put up with in order to transport those goods to market.
How can we succeed under that? Again, I come back to my original theory. If we are going to have faith in this nation, we have got to correct some of those inequities and not just sit back and complain about it. I wish some of us were on the government side of the House so we could do something about these issues. When we get there, we will clean it up.

May 22, 1991
The Address
We are no sooner reeling from the results of free trade with the United States than the government is running headlong into free trade with Mexico. We have already seen what can happen. Of the eight industries that left the town of Renfrew, in my riding, one was the Playtex plant. Some of that business went to Mexico because of cheap labour. Some went to parts of the Far East. Those interests go wherever the low wages are.
What are we going to do to handle that? Are we going to lower our wages in this country down to poorhouse wages? We have more faith in ourselves than that. We may have to adjust and do other things we can do better. It has to be done.
The government had promised that company that it was going to take the tax off the raw material that came into Canada from the United States. So the company thought: "Great, we will stay in Canada". It waited until after the free trade agreement was passed, and what happened? The tax on the raw material coming in from New Jersey, or wherever, was not taken off. So the company felt betrayed and left.
Those are just some examples. It is true that there is a big link between the economy and national unity in this country, as I said in the beginning. It is too bad it has taken the government so long to find that out.
I was delighted to see the recognition in the throne speech, just as I was delighted to see our leader's term: "the Canada round", referring to the next round of negotiations to try to amend our Canadian Constitution and create a base for national unity.
The term "Canada round" was used by the leader of the Liberal Party months before this throne speech came into play. We do not mind them picking up some of our good points. We can give them lots of good points if they would use them. We hope they will.
It is too bad the government is seen to be so eager to produce quickly with free trade agreements. With the deindustrialization of places like Ontario, with what has happened to the lumber industry, as I have outlined, you almost begin to wonder whether this government really knows for which nation it is the national government.
We see the trucking industry in the United States getting preference over our industry and the forest industry getting preference. I just want to say here that on the defence side there are all kinds of contracts. The Americans are holding back some of those contracts for themselves in the United States. Are we really on a free trade basis?
This government was elected in 1984 and stated that it was going to do everything possible for the Department of National Defence. We heard all these great comments, but the fact remains that the defence department personnel certainly are not very proud of what the government is doing for them now.
It wants them to go abroad. It wants them to go into the Persian Gulf and anywhere in the world for peacekeeping. When the soldiers came home from the Persian Gulf, the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence and the Associate Minister of National Defence were all there shaking hands with them when they came off the plane.
About two weeks later, they said: "We are going to cut you by 25 per cent." That was their reward. Some of these things have great effect on the regional development of this country. The then Minister of National Defence even mentioned this while some of the troops were still in the Persian Gulf. You can imagine what encouragement that gave to them.
Regional development involves post offices and various industries, government departments and so on.

After the previous Minister of Finance had the gall to say in August 1984: "We don't have to increase taxes to pay off the deficit or pay off the national debt. All we have to do is cancel government programs". The government has cancelled programs day in and day out. It has raised the taxes of this country 33 times since taking office and it has not made an impact. The national debt is still going up by leaps and bounds. That is the kind of managers these people are. It is time they are the customers rather than the managers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to talk about the subject of
Canadian unity, the theme in the Speech from the Throne.
It has been said many times, but I think most Canadians realize that this is a critical and difficult time in the constitutional history of Canada. Most Canadians are coming to the realization that it is a fact of life and something that we will have to come to grips with, that there will have to be a constitutional accommodation within Canada. I think that can be a very healthy thing.
When you look at the Canadian Constitution, there is no particular reason why an individual should be married under provincial law and divorced under federal law. Hopefully a look at our constitutional documents will yield a new accommodation that will make more sense and will be to the benefit of the Canadian Confederation. It is going to be a difficult job and everyone knows that.
Sometimes partisan considerations can get in the way of making a good accommodation for Canada. I do not denigrate partisan politics. I take pride in the fact that I am a partisan. I love partisan debate. I love the Progressive Conservative Party and I have been a member of it since my childhood but, at the same time, I do not think that either my partisan views or the partisan views of other members should get in the way of coming to the accommodation that we will need in Canada.
Let me give you an example of what I am talking about. I remember, shortly after my election in 1984, sitting down with one my constituents who was very much identified with a political party other than my own. It became obvious after awhile that it was very difficult, these partisan differences between the two of us, to talk about what, in effect, was a mutual problem. After awhile I said to the man involved, "Look, let's make a deal here. I am not going to look for your vote. I do not expect your vote. I am going to take a chance that I will not win or lose the 1988 election by one or more votes. So let's you and I agree that you are not going to try and change me because you will not. Let us get on with the problem and see if there is something that we can come up with."
I do not think that is a bad way for Canadians to proceed. Quite apart from whatever their perceptions are of me or the Progressive Conservative Party, this government or of politicians, it should not colour their perceptions about the need to come to an acceptable solution to Canada's constitutional needs.
May 22, 1991

If we can solve that, there will always be plenty of time. We have a long, great democratic tradition in this country where there will always be room and time for partisan politics, but this is too important an issue for that. I believe the stakes are very, very high.
I was at a meeting of the Royal Canadian Legion, the Stanford branch, several weeks ago. One of the veterans there, a man by the name of Frank Simon who lost an arm in World Word II, told me and those assembled that night that the veterans had fought for all of Canada, had fought for all of the provinces and all the territory of Canada, and the veterans, he said, are counting on the politicians and, indeed, all Canadians to keep this country together. I think those are good words to remember in this debate because when all is said and done, this is a wonderful country. You only have to visit other countries in the world, you only have to talk to any of the people who come into our office who want to emigrate to Canada, to know just how lucky we are as Canadians. I think it is important that we remind ourselves of that sometimes.
All of us have had conversations where we dwell on the problems that Canada is facing. All of us have letters that enumerate all the things that are wrong with Canada. Of all the letters I get, the ones that bother me the most are not the ones that criticize me personally. They are not the ones that criticize this government. They are not the ones that criticize politicians. They are the letters and comments that seem to take aim at Canada itself. Those are the ones I find very difficult and upsetting, even after being in this business for six or seven years.
What I say to them, to all Canadians, and to my constituents is: "Okay, there are many problems in Canada. I think we can solve them". Perhaps we have even made a list of all the things we think are wrong with Canada. But in every argument there is another side. Is it not equally valid, once we have talked about all the provinces, to talk about all the great things about Canada? Is that not equally valid? I think it is.
Whenever I mention the wonderful things in Canada, the obvious counter argument is: "Well, there are still problems with that. It is not perfect". To which I reply: "The list of things that are absolutely no problems or the list of things that are perfect is a very, veiy short list". If we acknowledge that, which can be the perennial criticism, we should talk about, we should list, and we should
The Address
think within ourselves as Canadians about all the things that make Canada the great country it is, if we could possibly list them.
I have been saying to people for many, many years that we have the best health care system in the world. The best health care system in the world is right here in Canada. People say that there are problems with it, that it is not perfect. I acknowledge that it is the best in the world, right here in Canada.
This parliamentary system is one of the wonderful things about Canada. This is an open system. This is a Parliament that gives an opportunity to individuals who are not rich or are not born into an aristocracy. This Parliament is open to all who have ambition and who have something to say about Canada. That is one of the wonderful things about Canada.
We can check all the judicial systems in the world, but I know of none better at balancing the public interest and individual rights than our judicial system.
We have an open, accessible, affordable education system in Canada.
Someone said to me recently: "The geography and climate in Canada mean that we are spared most of the natural disasters we read about almost every night in the paper. Those are things we should be thankful for". However, if this country is going to pull together, if it is going to solve the problems we face, it will take all of us looking at the big picture. It will take all of us looking beyond whether we like politicians. It will not just be politicians that will be able to solve this. We need the special interest groups that will say: "Okay, let us look at the greater good of Canada at the same time as looking at our needs".
We will have to ask the media to say: "There is a bigger picture here".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments with regard to the hon. member's speech.
First of all, I think most members would probably agree with him in the sense that the constitutional debate should be a non-partisan type of debate. I would tend to agree with that also. But the difficulty I have with that and the difficulty that people have with that are the actions of the present government.
The present government, as I see it and as many Canadians see it, has contributed to the problem in Canada. It has contributed to disunity, mistrust and the loss of confidence in the system. Rather than developing the proper attitude and esprit that is necessary, this government has been dismantling many of the institutions that have kept us united over the years.
I can mention the CBC, VIA Rail cuts, and even Canada Post. In many areas in Canada the only federal presence they have in their communities is the post office with the Canadian flag on it. Right at the present moment, even in my own area of Restigouche-Chaleur and in northern New Brunswick, we see what they are doing to Canada Post. Recent announcements indicate the possibility of laying off 11 workers in an area where the unemployment rate is 18.5 per cent. They are going to lay off 11 workers for the sake of rationalization. There is no way that Canada Post can convince me that it is going to be more efficient to send mail 200 miles east to be sorted only to come back west later. At the present time it is being sorted right in that area and then sent directly west.
I find it very difficult to believe that it will be a non-partisan debate. I hope it will be for the sake of the country, but now the biggest malaise out there is not necessarily a mistrust in the politicians but a mistrust in
this government. They see that the government has contributed to the problem of unity in this country and dismantled many of our national institutions that were there to keep our country united.
Does the hon. member agree with the type of program that his government is carrying out in the sense that it has announced cutbacks in public servants, some 90,000 of them since its mandate started? It is proud of that and wants to continue that. Does he agrees with the Canada Post policy of completely closing down rural post offices?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express my appreciation for the opportunity to take part in this throne speech debate and to express some of my concerns arising from the government's current economic and other policies which I believe are contributing to the state of this country today and are tearing this country apart.
May 22, 1991

I listened with interest to the speech of the member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke. It is important to understand that many Canadians, when they express concern about the unity of the country, are concerned about the economic issues and their status within the national economy. I think that is a serious part of the problem this country is facing today.
I listened to the Minister of Communications when he opened the debate today. He talked about what the Fathers of Confederation were facing in the period between 1864 to 1867 when as the Minister of Communications said they were looking at putting or stitching together a disparate set of colonies with stitches or ribbons of steel.
I am not sure that when he talked about the vision of those Fathers of Confederation that that was actually the vision they had. I think the Fathers of Confederation were probably more concerned at the time in addressing the economic and various social problems they were facing as partisan politicians of the day. They were trying to deal with the problems of their relations with the United States economy, trying to deal with the problems of transportation and communications within what was then British North America, trying to deal with the problems of two very disparate cultures that existed in the North America of the day. Essentially, they were not politicians with long-term visions; they were pragmatic politicians who were trying to deal with the problems they perceived were facing British North America at the time they set out on their project of nation building.
The other thing in the process of nation building that these politicians were facing was the fact that they were operating against the natural geography of North America. Those disparate colonies that the Minister of Communications was talking about were in essence extensions of the geographic systems of North America: the Atlantic provinces are an extension of Appalachia; central Canada is an extension of the central United States.
They were trying to create a nation in British North American that ran contrary to the normal and natural boundaries and process of human communication within the geographic areas of North America.
The Address
It was a great challenge. It was an inspiring challenge to those of us who are trying to deal with similar problems in the current day because what those politicians were attempting to do was ignore the natural boundaries of North America and create a nation which, rather than running from north to south, ran from east to west across the natural barriers of the country.
Given what they had to work with I think they did a terrific job. The Canada of today is a tribute to the foresight of those Fathers of Confederation and also of subsequent Parliaments which generally followed in their pragmatic footsteps. To the credit of the founders of the Canadian nation they ignored those natural boundaries, the pressures and the pulls from the United States, and they created this country of Canada.
I think they had to recognize, Mr. Speaker, as you and I have to recognize today, that we are living in the third largest national state in the world, one of the largest countries on the globe. We have a very small population, 27 million people spread in general over a tiny belt of land adjacent to the United States boundary. The logistics of trying to create, manage, and sustain a country that is built on that basis is very difficult for any Parliament, for any government, for any politician and it requires a tremendous amount of pragmatism, of looking at the problems facing you, the circumstances facing you, and dealing in real terms with those problems.
I think over the years that is precisely what we have had. We have been well served by parliaments in terms of their pragmatic approach in dealing with this country-which defies national order-and keeping this country together.
We have been, I think the operative word is pragmatic. Unfortunately, within the last few years, governments have tended to become more and more ideological. In those terms they are following the political culture of the United States, which is becoming more and more polarized in terms of right wing politicians and liberal politicians. As a consequence it appears that the government in this country is becoming more and more oriented to the kind of free market theory that seems to have been adopted by the Reagan Republicans in the United States.

May 22, 1991
The Address
It is that orientation towards the free market theory that has undermined and destroyed the pragmatism that generally governed politicians in this country up to the present government. As a result, we are seeing the forces that are tearing this country apart coming from an ideological commitment and from a dismissing of the pragmatic approach to governing Canada.
As the Fathers of Confederation saw it, Canada was a very large land mass that had to be held together to support a very small population. Well, how do you do that? You cannot do it simply with private investment because no investor in his or her right mind would invest money in such a very small market distributed over such a very large land area. So there was a necessity for government involvement in these kinds of investments.
The Government of Canada became involved in the building of the national railway system. Essentially it was a joint venture between private entrepreneurs and the Government of Canada, so there was public money as well as private money involved in what the Minister of Communications called that ribbon of steel that stitched the colonies of British North America together.
In addition, when the time came to have an airline in Canada, that initiative did not come from the private sector because there was not sufficient market to serve in order for the private sector to make a profit. The Government of Canada became involved and set up the trans-Canada airlines system, which became Air Canada.
The government also became involved in other areas of transportation and communications. The post office became a communications system that extended through every part of Canada, as our leader likes to say, from coast to coast to coast. You could send a letter to any part of Canada whether you sent it next door or you sent it up to northern Canada, it could all be done at the same rate. All Canadians have the right to communicate with their fellow Canadians on an equal basis.
All of these things were done through government investment, because the government and the pragmatic politicians of the day realized that if they were going to keep a small population welded together into a nation
over the huge land mass that is Canada, it was going to require a more pragmatic approach than could be provided by the ideologies of the day.
One of the problems that Canada is facing today is that they have an extremely ideological government that ignores the pragmatic requirements of this country and in fact has adopted economic policies that are tearing the country apart.
What has this government done? It has virtually eliminated passenger rail service in the country. That ribbon of steel that the Minister of Communications was talking about no longer serves Canadians in the same way that it served Canadians before. There is no continuous passenger service across this country because the Tories in applying their marketplace test to that institution, decided it did not meet the test. It may have met the national unity test; it may have been important from the point of view of national unity, but the Tories decided that it did not meet the marketplace test and therefore they undermined the VIA Rail passenger service that was used as a link to keep Canadians together from one end of the countiy to the other.
The same thing is happening with the post office. It used to be that if you went to any community in Canada, from the east coast to the west coast, to the north coast, there was Canada Post with the name of the community on the side and with the Canadian flag flying overhead. This party with its ideological rigidity decided that even though the post office system met the test of national unity, something that Canadians could perceive as an institution in their community, whether they lived in eastern Canada, western Canada, northern Canada, central Canada, it did not meet the market test.
Therefore, the Conservatives dismantled the Canada Post system by privatizing rural post offices, by putting postal services into Seven-11 stores in communities all over the province. When we go to buy our stamps, money orders and pick up our parcels and mail, where do we pick it up? Do we pick it up in an institution with the Canadian flag flying overhead? No, we pick it up in a private enterprise store owned by the Southland Corporation of the United States.
May 22, 1991

In that way they undermine the unity of this country for market reasons, for ideological reasons. It has created serious divisions between Canadians, serious divisions within the Canadian community. The same thing has happened with virtually every other national institution that was put together, not with a market test in mind but with the national unity test in mind in order to keep this country together.
It is unfortunate that the Tories have allowed themselves to be strictly hidebound to this market test, to this ideological test while ignoring the requirements for national unity.
As the Fathers of Confederation determined, sometimes it does not make sense in terms of geography and the economy to build a nation where there was not a nation before. Sometimes it required a commitment beyond the market test. They challenged that commitment, they met that commitment and they built this nation.
Now unfortunately what we are perceiving in the Conservative economic policy is that they simply apply the market test, whether it is to CBC, whether it is to VIA Rail, whether it is to Air Canada, whether it is to Petro-Canada, and they have failed to apply the national unity test. As a result they are dismantling many of the national institutions that Canadians perceive as necessary to keep this country together.
One of the serious cracks that have occurred in the system of national unity in the last few years is as a result of the so-called free trade agreement between Canada and the United States.
Before I discuss that, I want to discuss social policy because it is not simply the concrete and the steel, and the communication and transportation systems that are the bulwarks of national unity in this country. Pragmatic politicians in later days also saw that there was a necessity to maintain a consistent standard of social programs across Canada so that someone who entered a hospital in the provinces of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, or someone who entered hospital in the provinces of British Columbia, Ontario or Quebec, could enjoy the same standard of care regardless of where they entered that hospital.
The same is true of social programs, such as welfare, child support and that kind of thing. The same is true of old age pensions and family allowances. All of these things became a part of the bulwark of national unity so that Canadians in one part of the country felt they were equal in terms of the benefits they received from the
The Address
government as Canadians in any other part of the country.
Conservative economic policy, based on Conservative ideology, rather than on a pragmatic need to keep this country together, to sustain and to maintain it has begun to tear that system of social benefits apart, so that soon in the ultimate goal of this Tory ideology is to disassemble that system of social benefits so that some Canadians benefit more than others or some Canadians in some regions of this country are going to benefit more than others.
The result of that dismantling of social policies, of that bulwark of national unity is going to be threats to national unity, a decline in the sense of nationhood among Canadians because of the feeling that some Canadians are going to benefit more greatly than others.
The same thing has happened with Tory fiscal policy, with taxation policy. I think everybody who reads the statistics of Statistics Canada will know that the changes in the tax system, the so-called tax reform that this party has brought out, have resulted in the rich in this country becoming richer and more secure while the poor in this country have become poorer and less secure.
I ask you members, sitting in the House here today, how you would feel about a Canada that treats rich people differently than poor people, one that oppresses its poor people and makes the rich people richer. You will not have a very good sense about Canada if you are one of the millions of poor people and poor children in this country who see the system treating them unequally.
Before we get involved in the discussions around national unity which look at the Constitution, the distribution of powers and the mechanics of amending the Constitution, we must walk back through the damage that the Conservative Party has done over the last few years, since 1984, to the economic system in this country.
I think Canadians have always felt that, almost exclusively among countries in the world, in this country there was at least a measure of fairness from their government and that they would not be taxed more heavily than other Canadians or would not be excused from taxes because they enjoyed a certain amount of wealth or power. Canadians always felt that there was a certain amount of fairness in a progressive tax system; that the benefits they received from this country would be received equally and fairly no matter where you lived across the country. Family allowances were the same in Nova Scotia as they were in British Columbia. All of those benefits were fairly distributed.

May 22, 1991
The Address
The Tories have begun to tinker with and undermine that system. As a result, many Canadians feel that there are now different gradations of Canadians, different classes of Canadians and that some people benefit to a greater extent while others pay to a greater extent. That is not the way to encourage national unity.
I would encourage the current government to examine some of its social policies and some of the policies that it has brought about over the last few years and find out how they have contributed to undermining a sense of national unity among Canadians. It is not too late to change those policies, to reverse them and to start moving back toward a system in which Canadians feel equally treated by the Government of Canada and equally responsible toward maintaining this country and maintaining the unity of this country because they certainly do not now. It does not matter where you go in this country, there are people who feel they are unfairly treated by the federal government and that some people are treated much better.
Once we restore the balance and restore the equity, we can start talking to people convincingly about national unity. We certainly cannot do it until then.

Mr. Speaker, I was very surprised at some of the comments made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
First of all, his view of the Fathers of Confederation surprises me, coming from a Socialist member. He saw them and the birth of Canada as part of a great vision. There was no thought of a great symbol of unity or a great vision. Financial guarantees were needed on the London market, and these very wealthy capitalists made a lot of money on the railroads with the guarantees they got from the people. So this had nothing to do with a great vision for the people of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to give my response to the Speech from the Throne.
The throne speech addressed three major concerns of Canadians: unity, prosperity and government responsiveness. All are intertwined.
The fragility of unity becomes apparent when our economy falters. It has also become apparent as our national debt has grown, compound interest on compound interest. We as a government must address these economic matters. We must also address the constitutional matters, and we are.
Today I would like to speak about Canadian unity from a different perspective. It is a narrow perspective, but it is one of utmost importance. I would like to discuss the importance of Canadian symbols.
I agree with all the debaters before me who have talked about the health of the economy and the structure of the Constitution and division of powers. Those are of paramount importance. However, we as Canadians have symbols. We must look back at what has united us as a country and at our common historical reality.
We have many, many symbols in this country. We have the flag, we have our institutions, we have common celebrations like Expo '67 and the Centennial celebrations of 1967. We will have one in 1992. We have common rituals, such as the singing of the anthem and the citizenship ceremony. All of these create a feeling of patriotism. We should increase and expand our use of symbols so we can quietly be proud of what we have achieved as a nation and as Canadians. These are positive things we can do to unite our country and our people.
All too often we forget about the benefits we have enjoyed as Canadians and our accomplishments as Canadians. I have been fortunate enough to do a little travelling. When I am in other countries, I realize how good we have it in Canada and for how much we have to be thankful.
We look inward as Canadians, when often we should be looking outward. We have made contributions to peace and freedom through two World Wars, the Boer War, the Korean War and the recent war. Our achievements continue. These are the achievements of Roy Brown and Billy Bishop.
Next year, Canada will celebrate its 125th birthday. In 1927, Canada celebrated its 60th birthday. At that time, celebrations were held and Canadians rejoiced about Canada and the contributions they made to the world.
The Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII, toured Canada to celebrate our Diamond Jubilee. That year, the Confederation Building, which is part of the House of Commons, was opened. It was to commemorate Canada's 50th birthday. During Canada's 50th birthday we were involved in a war and celebrations were postponed for 10 years.
Canada should commemorate our 125th birthday by opening our Parliament Buildings to Canadians. The Parliament Buildings are one of the most important symbols we have as Canadians. They have become crowded, overused and overworked.
There are plans to reallocate space and build a visitor reception centre in the basement in the entrance under the Peace Tower, where there could be a theatre, public washrooms and some displays. We should do this without hesitation or trepidation. A small expenditure like this is money which is not wasted.
The Government of Canada should help Canadians to recognize their achievements by building symbols like statues and monuments. For example, we could participate with the city of Edmonton to build a statue to commemorate the achievements of the five women who pursued the Persons case-Louise McKinney, Henrietta Edwards, Nellie McClung, Emily Murphy and Irene
May 22, 1991

Parlby. These women's historic accomplishment was in pursuing the right for women to vote. They took the case all the way to the Privy Council of London, England.
The Government of Canada should not be afraid to erect a statue of these women on the lawn of the Supreme Court. We may want to commemorate other historical figures. For example, those Canadians who have won the Victoria Cross. We think of them fleetingly on November 11 each year. Why, for example, could we not erect statues of Victoria Cross winners in the towns and cities of their birth? Perhaps we could erect one or two each year to ground in reality our achievements as Canadians and to celebrate our common historical experience.
Canadians are imaginative and we, as a government, should share in their sense of how to recognize Canadian achievements. It seems only prudent to ask Canadians to come up with ideas on how to do this.
The confusion of our historical reality manifests itself in the fact that departments and ministers create award after award to recognize achievements of Canadians. For example, the Secretary of State has a National Volunteer Award. The Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council has recently established a gold medal for science.
We see a proliferation of awards throughout departments and ministers. There are awards for business excellence and many other awards. Perhaps as a government we should take a look at these awards and bring them together under one administrative unit and then re-examine what we are doing and where we are going.
We have national institutions in Ottawa which people rarely see. We should try to bring our national institutions out to Canadians. For example, why should many of the National Art Gallery's treasures be locked away in storage? Could there not be more travelling exhibitions, more co-operative exhibitions with galleries across the country? Perhaps we might even consider building branch plants: a western art gallery or an eastern national art gallery.
The same could be said of our other institutions such as the Museum of Civilization and the Museum of Science and Technology.
Canadians feel very proud when we think of our international accomplishments such as peacekeeping, fighting apartheid, or emergency relief. We give aid to developing countries but Canadians complain that the money might be better spent at home.
The Address
We help countries to develop their economies, train their people and protect the environment. This is largely unknown to Canadians. I believe we must recognize in Canada our international accomplishments.
We have to achieve much more. For example, the member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore has suggested that Canada aggressively pursue the idea of an international green cross, an international environmental disaster clean-up organization. I think this is where we could symbolize our achievements to the world, and I believe that the government should pursue this with vigour.
We might also think of pursuing with the United Nations an international environmental agency, something along the lines of the International Atomic Energy Agency. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the International Atomic Energy Agency provides expert advice to countries as well as funding to develop nuclear energy. It also serves as an enforcement agency in checking to make sure that the countries adhere to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
We might develop an international environmental agency along the same lines. This environmental agency could provide expert advice as well as funding to developing nations on environmental matters such as energy efficiency and renewable energy. It could also serve to set and enforce minimum environmental standards.
We have much to offer the world. As a middle power we are limited in what we can do, but perhaps we can stretch our boundaries to move beyond our well-known and effective traditional intermediary role.
I would like to close by reiterating that we as a country should continue to build our symbols and continue to develop and share our common historical reality with Canadians so that we can be proud of our accomplishments.

May 22, 1991
The Address
However, I want to ask him about two things. When we look at the Canadian symbols we could perhaps recognize that the Speech from the Throne does not particularly relate to all the issues that he talked about. Could the hon. member consider that we have to honour those people who have contributed to the two world wars and to the history of Canada by putting some financial wherewithal into our Canadian Museum of History, the national monuments as he has pointed out? I think they are seriously underfinanced.
To date we have been busy building museums in most of Canada, particularly in Quebec, and I think we have ignored one of the most important major symbols that has united us as a country.
The second symbol which I would ask him to address is: What would he do if he were the minister with respect to the Canadian broadcasting system? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak in the debate on the Speech from the Throne.
This is a very important juncture in our country's history. We are faced with gargantuan problems as a nation and as politicians. Following our recent recess, it was reasonable for the people of Canada to assume that the government was going to deal with these problems
in a meaningful way in the Speech from the Throne. Unfortunately, all we have are meaningless platitudes and generalities, not coming anywhere near what is necessary to deal with the daunting problems with which we are faced.
The major concerns of Canadians are not addressed. The major concerns of Canadians today are high taxation, unemployment, the Constitution, and the environment. Yet we see in the Speech from the Throne mere generalities and conversation. Where is the fodder, the seed needed to develop answers to the problems that we have as a nation? It is completely absent. This government has indicated that the problems of the country are not first and foremost in its mind. What it hopes to do is be able to skate through the next few months and hopefully along the way, by perhaps tapping into a poll here and there, be able to generate some answer that will be pleasing and meet the approval of the Canadian public.
The Canadian public is not going to be fooled. The Canadian public realizes the seriousness of the problems that face this nation at the present time. The Canadian public realizes, as we do here in this House of Commons, the possibilities of this great country. Yet these possibilities are not being honoured by this government. The government is completely sloughing off the duty which is before it at the present time.
What is it sloughing off, what does it refuse to deal with? Well, it essentially refuses to deal with problems that are of its making. This is what most annoys Canadians. The government entered into a trade agreement with the United States. Now it is talking about a tripartite trade agreement with the United States and Mexico. Yet the trade agreement with the United States is a very ill-conceived document in many ways.
What is happening as a result? We have not received the benefits of the trade agreement that were promised by the government. In fact, we are losing industry to the United States. States from the United States are setting up offices in Canada, presumably trade delegations, with the main purpose of influencing and encouraging Canadian industry to move south of the border. They are doing it. We are not competing with the United States. Our industries are leaving Canada because of high interest rates, because we are not providing for Canadians what the Americans insisted on having for their own businesses and their own citizens. That is a level playing field.
The government would have us believe that we have high interest rates as a result of inflation.
May 22, 1991

That is part of the reason for high interest rates, but the main reason for high interest rates is that the government has to sell Treasury bonds. The government has to sell bonds to pay the interest on the debt. The reason the government is doing this is because it has not found the answers it promised the Canadian public it would find in the 1984 election campaign. It was horrified that a debt existed in Canada, it was horrified that the debt was approximately $170 billion in 1984.
This summer the debt of this nation will reach $400 billion. Four hundred billion dollars. The government says: "Well, don't look to us, we inherited this problem". The fact that it is almost more than double what it was when this government came to power is not important to the government. It sees this as incidental. It sees the fact that the deficit was there, albeit a much smaller deficit, as the most important thing.
The government will say to us: "We couldn't deal with it, we inherited it, it is not our fault". I would say to the government that it more than doubled the debt in a period of time when the economy of Canada was in very, very good shape indeed. We were going through very good economic times between 1984 and 1990.
If the government is saying it could not deal with the debt at that time, when can we as a nation deal with it? Can we deal with it now, when the government through its poor and misguided economic policies has plunged us into a made-in-Canada recession? No, we cannot. We cannot do it now. Of course, we have to be mindful of spending. However, the fact that the debt has been allowed to grow to $400 billion because this government did not keep its word to the Canadian public has put in peril the programs that this country holds dear, that this country holds as pillars of its society and foundations of the Canadian way of life.
We are now in a position of listening to the government question programs that we as Canadians had reason to believe would be there-hard fought programs which the Liberal government put in place, such as the national medical plan and the old age pensions.
These are programs that Canadians now feel are not solid. They look to the government saying: "My heavens, you have broken the promise of solidifying the economy of this country. You told us that there was not going to be any danger to the programs that we fought for and won. Now, we look at the situation that exists in Ottawa and
The Address
we are afraid, afraid for our Canadian programs, and afraid for our social programs. We are very concerned about where this country is going".
If it was the plan of the Government of Canada to do away with our social programs, it could not have handled it any better than the government did. The economic mess it created put the Canadian public in a position where they assume that anything can happen. This is a very sad legacy indeed.
No wonder politicians are just one notch above loan sharks in the minds of the Canadian public, when they see what this government has done in taking the country of tomorrow, as we liked to regard Canada, and jettisoning its future, its immediate future. No wonder the Canadian public is upset. They have every reason to be upset.
What has the high interest rate done? The high interest rate has created a high Canadian dollar. That was the whole idea, to make our Treasury bonds attractive. Of course, it has also raised the value of the Canadian dollar. What do we have now as a legacy from this government? We do not have a solid commercial economy. We do not have a solid commercial and industrial base. We have, thanks to this government, ever increasing cross-border shopping. Cross-border shopping is a situation that is going to devastate the border towns and communities in Canada.
Why is it happening? It is because the people of this country are fed up. They are showing their distaste and anger with the government by getting into their automobiles and driving into the United States. This could be corrected if we could reduce the value of the Canadian dollar to where it should be. Then the products in the United States would be more expensive and there would be no incentive to go to the United States. We cannot because the government refuses to reduce interest rates and the resulting high Canadian dollar.
Because of the high Canadian dollar and high interest rates, businesses in Canada are finding it very difficult to compete. They are finding it difficult to sell into the United States. They are moving into the United States because they find they can have reduced expenses if they are located in the United States, and this is not helping Canada.
Whether we get out of this recession this year or next year, we are going to be faced with a smaller number of commercial enterprises in this country. We are going to lose these industries and organizations. This is going to be another sad legacy of this government and another problem with which the Canadian public will be faced.

May 22, 1991
The Address
We entered into a trade agreement with the United States that did not define a subsidy. We do not have a subsidy. We have five to seven years to determine what a subsidy is. A subsidy is not defined. It is defined in the minds of the American people, the American agencies and the American government. They know when Canadians receive a subsidy.
I have a plant in my riding, Sydney Steel Corporation, that is being subsidized because it received federal and provincial government assistance in the 1970s and the early 1980s, long before the free trade agreement was even contemplated with the United States. It is being countervailed against because the Americans are saying that this company received a subsidy.
What about the tax free period of time being offered by the United States to industries that will leave southern Ontario and relocate? What about the free land that is being offered in industrial parks to have these industries move to the United States? Are those subsidies? Of course they are subsidies. Our government is not sticking up for and protecting the Canadian commercial base the way the Americans are obviously protecting their industry and their economic future.
We are saying: "If the Americans want to do it, it has got to be fine, it has got to be great". I am not criticizing the Americans. The American government is obviously sticking up for its own people and its own commercial base. All I am saying is: Why is our government not doing something to protect the Canadian economy? Why are we leaving? Why are we jettisoning our Canadian public?
Something has gone wrong here. What has gone wrong is that this government does not know what to do. No wonder it cannot put anything in a Speech from the Throne. It does not know what it wants to do.
All of the points I have made are to me and to most Canadians extremely serious. The most serious economic difficulty we face is our constitutional problem. Fortunately, we still have investment that can be made in Canada, but a lot of people who would like to invest in Canada will not invest in Canada with this uncertainty with respect to our constitutional future and our unity is up in the air.
What is the government doing? It is dragging its feet. The government is saying: "Well, we are going to bring forward a plan in the fall." Then it says: "Now don't you say anything, opposition, because we want this to be non-partisan." If you are a Canadian and you feel for this country and you see that this government is doing
absolutely nothing to try to correct the differences and to try to bring this country together, you have got to say something. You have got to complain that you feel frustrated by what is going on, that we are just marking time and we are going to roll the dice perhaps at the last minute to try and solve the problem again.
You have got to say something to voice your disapproval. According to the government, if you do you are being partisan. Well, I am being partisan because I find that what this government has done is woefully inadequate. It is woefully inadequate to deal with the problems that face this country; the unity question and the economy. How is this government going to deal with the problems of the future if it cannot deal with the problems of the present? What are we going to do with our environment?
The government has a green plan. That was deep sixed like nothing we have ever seen. It saw the light of day and like the groundhog, it saw its shadow and went back underground again. The whole question of the environment is just a real bad joke in this country. We have a very serious environmental concern in Canada and this government is saying: "Wait now, we do not want to get this started. We may be starting something here we are not really ready to handle." It is saying that this is something that can wait. Well, it cannot wait.
Child care in this country cannot wait. This government cannot define economic success and it cannot see that what it has created is an economic hole for itself. It cannot see that regional disparity is increasing. It is referring now to the 1990s in Nova Scotia as the mean decade. It sees transfer payments being cut off. It sees equalization payments disappearing. It sees regional development as a thing of the past. We are losing our support from the federal government. It is now talking about closing more bases in Atlantic Canada. It is closing bases when it does not even have a defence policy. How does it know what to close? It does not know what it is doing.
This is chaos, this is not government. People of Canada are concerned and they have every reason to be concerned.
How can the Canadian public possibly even consider supporting this government in a subsequent election? What the people of Canada want is action. They want us to bring back the Canada that was being evolved through years of hard work by politicians and by Canadians. They do not want the government to deep-six the future of this country. They want the government to deal with the questions. They want their concerns addressed. They do not want any more burying of the problems. They do not want Parliament just to sit every now and then. They do

not want the government to be more concerned with polls and public opinion than with the needs of Canadians.
Canadians have a right to have their concerns addressed and it is time this government realized it and it is time this government did something about it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, another interesting talk by a member opposite who has a very deep insecurity problem because what I heard as I listened, and I did tty to listen to everything that the hon. member said, was a lot of worry, a lot of doubt and a lot of basic inability to come to terms with reality as it is in the world today.
I guess that inability to come to terms with reality is part of what was wrong with the Liberal government prior to 1984, when it was in power over such a long period of time, when it developed a burdensome debt that we are still trying to get out from under and left a legacy in this country that probably our children and perhaps even our grandchildren will still be dealing with.
I am not surprised, given the sense of insecurity and self-doubt that the hon. member epitomizes on behalf of his party, that they were so incapable of dealing with these problems and these challenges in the past.
Fortunately, the electorate saw the light and elected a government that does have a plan, a government that does have the ability to take the kind of action that the hon. member calls for and a government that has the courage to do things that are necessary, even when perhaps they are unpopular, because we know that we must do what is right over what is perceived to be popular.
I would suggest to the hon. member that change is precisely what we have created in this country. We have done these things, taken these actions that the hon. member calls for. We have addressed some of the problems that were burdening the economy of this country. Maybe our reward for that is to be at perhaps less than a desirable point in the polls right now, but I think that really just points to the fact that there is courageous ability on this side of the House to take the kinds of actions that are necessary.
The Address
Our job is to create a climate of security, a climate of hope, a sense of a future for this country where people will be prepared to make the kinds of investments that are necessary to ensure our prosperity in the future. I suggest that is the positive kind of action we are taking.
I would just ask the hon. member opposite if he would tell us what the Liberal government would do to reduce interest rates below the already low rate they are at, at around 9 per cent, when in their term of government, interest rates reached the all time high of over 22 per cent.

The hon. member also talks about the Canadian electorate as if the Canadian electorate has bestowed some kind of support upon them, a party at 14 per cent. Something about reality is that the deficit this year is $30.5 billion. It is as high as it has ever been. This was a government that was going to reduce the deficit. There are 5 million poor people in Canada. That is reality. There are 1.5 million unemployed. That is reality, and
1.8	million Canadians depend on food banks. That is reality. That is the reality that this government has imposed on this country.

In my constituency, in industrial Cape Breton, the unemployment rate is 22 per cent. That is the figure that Statistics Canada will admit to.
We are continually losing jobs. Our unemployment rate is growing constantly. Our young people are not coming back to Cape Breton. There are no jobs available. Our communities can no longer afford to provide the essential services that Canadians have every right to take for granted in this country.
We are in a deep problem in our municipalities. The future economically is of grave concern. To even suggest that this government has addressed these problems is ludicrous.
I would like to say that what Canadians want is hope. We still hope. We still hope that this government can change. speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak, albeit 10 to 20 minutes late. I want to thank you for recognizing me now.
I want to join my colleague from Edmonton-Strath-cona in expressing my pleasure in having the opportunity to speak to the address from the throne. The throne speech itself gives a blueprint for what the intentions of the government are for the rest of this Parliament. Partly it is built on the record of the past, and it looks backward, but it uses that backward look in order to establish a plan and a blueprint for the future.
In this particular throne speech the focus has been on unity and the economy. It is difficult to bring unity to a country and tranquillity to a nation when there are economic barriers to that kind of security that people long for. When unemployment is high, as it is in parts of Canada today, it is difficult for those people to think in terms of unity of the country, even though they want that for our land. Their first concern is for a job. When there
are business failures across Canada, it is difficult for those business people, who have experienced that loss, to think in terms of unity, even though that is one of their first desires. It is very important that we address the economic issues in our land together with the unity questions.
I want to say how pleased I am to be part of a government that has been making the tough decisions that should have been made years and decades ago in order to usher us into the 21st century and prepare us for that.
So much of what we have done in the last six or seven years has been in the nature of restructuring the nation, restructuring the economy so that we can be ready to move with the rest of the countries of the world into a new and emerging economy of the world. Therefore, we have been dealing with such things as pension reform so that our people can have confidence in the future for their own personal lives. We have been dealing with tax reform, whether it is sales tax, corporate tax or income tax. We have dealt with issues like tax reform so that our economy can adjust itself to the future competitiveness of our nation which we are are going to have to face if we are going to trade around the world.
We have dealt with trade liberalization because the world is changing. We cannot expect the world and the economies of the world and the trading patterns of the world to stay the same in order to accommodate us. If the rest of the world is changing, we have to change along with it in order to be competitive, in order to provide jobs, in order to provide the security that our people long for.
We have dealt with the restructuring of our economy and we have dealt with making our country as competitive as possible in order to help our people. When there is unemployment, when there is poverty, when there is any other difficulty, nowhere is it felt more keenly than at the level of the family. So I am pleased that the throne speech included a statement that dealt with a look at the family. It says:
In addition, my government will review its policies in relation to the family, the most fundamental building block of Canadian society.
"The most fundamental building block of Canadian society." Mr. Speaker, if we are going to have a confident, unified and sure approach to the future, we have to do it in the context of happy families, of sure and secure families.
May 22, 1991

There are probably a lot of people here in the House and across Canada who ask themselves why have we come back to the notion of the traditional family unit; why is the traditional family unit so important?
I want to take a minute just to commend the member for Calgary North for the extensive research he has done on the way the tax policies of our country have prejudiced the traditional family. I would commend his speech of May 15, pages 125 and 126 of Hansard, to members. They should look at how, since 1917, the tax policies of successive governments of Canada have ignored the pressures that tax policies are placing on the traditional family.
As I said, some people wonder why we keep harping on this. It is a part of reality to recognize that the family unit is not what it used to be. We can think of Leave it to Beaver or Father Knows Best or any number of those folksy kind of shows that were popular in the fifties and sixties, and think that that is the traditional family unit. Well, it is not that way.
Statistics show us that in the family today, in 62 per cent, both spouses are working; in 27 per cent, the husband only is working; in 7 per cent, neither husband nor wife is working; and in 4 per cent, only the wife is working. When we consider that in 62 per cent of the homes across Canada both husband and wife are working to make ends meet, we recognize that what we think of in a fanciful way as the traditional family no longer exists.
There are strains on the family, and it should not be the role of government to add to those strains. People ask; why is it so important to deal with family issues? I refer again to a gentleman whom I quote often, a famous sociologist from the University of Bordeaux, Jacques Ellal. He says that if a relationship is to be authentic, the other must be able to rely on the continuity of my behaviour, and know that he can expect certain kinds of words of help or refusals from me. Without such continuity, a relationship becomes impossible.
That is why the family unit is so important. The fact is that marriage introduces a regime of dependability in relationships. Dependability creates security, and security is important not only for the adults in the relationship, but for the children also.
The fact is that through the family we build the relationships that provide that security, but we also have
The Address
the vehicle that creates the transmission of values which are so very important for our society. Yet, as I indicated, and as my friend from Calgary North has pointed out so vividly, the tax policies of our governments through the years have created tensions for the family.
I quote an example from his speech on page 126. The family earns $60,000:
One family lives a traditional life-style and has one income and three children, two under seven and one child over seven. One of the parents cares for the children at home. They are married-The other family-is the same in every respect except that one of the younger children is unrelated to the others. Both parents work, earning $36,000 and $24,000, for a total of $60,000.
In the second example, the adults are not married.
It may seem incredible, but the total taxes paid by these two families differ by over $12,200. That is $1,000 per month more tax that the traditional family pays. Almost half of this can be related to the $36,000-$24,000 income split. The other half is due only to the fact that the traditional couple is married.
That is not the intention of any government. This began in 1917 and has carried on right to the present. It is important that our government take note of the fact that taxation policy is putting pressure on people who value the traditional family, who believe that tight, dependable, secure human relationships are important, who believe that children grow up best in families and who want to transmit their values through the family to the children.
It is important that we deal with this. I am happy to say that the Speech from the Throne indicates that the government is prepared to look at the traditional family as a building block for our society.
There is no doubt that poverty is an important question for our nation, but on this issue it is not a question of poverty. It is a question of fairness and taxation policies that deal fairly with all people. There should not be an advantage for one group of people over another.
I applaud the Prime Minister for taking this initiative to signal to the Canadian people and to the Parliament of Canada that he wants to see a regime introduced in Parliament whereby the traditional family is going to be dealt with equally with other families, and that the taxation policies of this government are not going to penalize those who want to build a traditional family unit.

May 22, 1991
The Address

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
