speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to take part in this debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
The speech pronounced by the Governor General on May 13 this year outlines the themes, principles and initiatives that the government intends to pursue in the months to come. Several journalists called this Speech from the Throne a straight repeat of the one pronounced on April 3, 1989.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, we find the same themes and the same ideas in both speeches. In other words, in the months to come, the government will follow the same path it has followed since it came to power in 1984. It promises to be a rocky road, if we consider the results of the initiatives announced in the Speech from the Throne in April 1989.
Canadians realize this, because the path this government forced us to take proved to be a dead end. For the first time in our history, we have a recession made in Canada by the Government of Canada. That is where we are now, thanks to the ideas set forth in the Speech from the Throne on April 3, 1989. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am concerned, because if the government intends to take the same path that led us into this recession, the situation can only get worse.
As I just pointed out, the present Speech from the Throne generally repeats the themes and objectives announced two years ago. Consider the four main objectives the government intended to pursue in its speech in April 1989.
The objectives mentioned were as follows: to build a strong economy; to preserve the environment; to maintain a caring, compassionate society; and finally, to renew the government's commitment to national unity.
Undoubtedly, these four objectives were, and still are, very noble and significant.
Unfortunately, the Conservative Government has failed miserably in these four major areas that are so important to the well-being of all Canadians.
Consider the first component of the April 1989 Speech from the Throne: to build a strong economy. Two years ago, the Conservative Government said it wanted to build a strong economy, encouraged by incentive. Today, the Conservatives seem to have been on the wrong track.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we are experiencing one of the worst economic recessions we ever had. This is not only a serious crisis but a crisis created by this government as a result of unsound economic policies.
The government's so-called incentives merely discouraged Canadians, Mr. Speaker. Just ask them. The incentives mentioned by the Tories two years ago merely worsened an economic situation already vulnerable as a result of high interest rates. Today, the Conservative Government says it has managed to bring down interest rates down, but it created this economic crisis by raising them in the first place.
In April 1989, the unemployment rate in Canada was
7.8	per cent. Today, it is 10.5 per cent. This is the highest unemployment rate since May 1985. In Montreal, the figures are even more depressing. In April 1989, the unemployment rate in the Montreal region was 9.7 per cent, and today, it is up to 14.2 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, the Montreal region has been severely affected by the economic crisis created by this Conservative Government. Today, nearly one out of four persons in Montreal, in other words, 25 per cent of the population, is living below the poverty line. This is shameful, Mr. Speaker. Across Quebec the situation is not much better. During the first months of 1991, the number of bankruptcies rose 40 per cent. According to Statistics Canada, 1,818 persons filed for protection under the Bankruptcy Act.
Clearly, the objectives pursued by this government since the April 1989 Speech from the Throne have done nothing to improve the lives of Canadians living in the Montreal region. If with this new Speech from the Throne, the government intends to follow the same path, the economic situation of the people of Montreal can only get worse.
In 1989, the then Minister of Finance promised that the deficit would go down to $28 billion. The exact opposite happened, Mr. Speaker: The deficit is now up to 30.5 billion. As far as the national debt is concerned, my leader, the Leader of the Opposition, explained in his speech how the Conservative Government had accumulated in only six years a debt equivalent to the debt accumulated in 117 years by all previous governments.
In the Speech from the Throne two years ago, the government told Canadians that it would offer incentives, but since then we have seen cuts in unemployment insurance benefits and cuts in the Job Development Program, subsidized housing and medicare.
May 22, 1991

This Speech from the Throne claims to help those in greatest need, but the truth is, this speech offers no respite for the unemployed, poor families, students who pay GST, the elderly or the sick. There is absolutely nothing in this Speech from the Throne that gives any hope to the neediest in our society. The government seems to be saying that the jobless will have to wait until the year 2000 to find jobs. That is unacceptable.
Mr. Speaker, the question we should be asking ourselves today if we give credence to the government's Speech from the Throne is this: what is going to happen to Montreal's 225,000 unemployed workers between now and the year 2000? Will they starve to death or will live with the hope that, one day, the sooner the better, they will be able to find a job and preserve their dignity? Cutbacks in all support programs during a time of crisis do little to inspire confidence.
Canadians are also sceptical about the latest Speech from the Throne. It states that the government wants to double the number of graduates in mathematics, the sciences and engineering to increase Canada's competitiveness. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that we need scientists and mathematicians if we want to encourage research and development. The fact remains that, in 1987, the total level of federal spending in research and development represented 1.4 percent of our GNP. Today, it is down to 1.28 percent, Mr. Speaker. Yet, I can remember well this Prime Minister stating loud and clear during the 1984 campaign, that he would double investment in research and development. Now, he has just reduced whathever little there was.
So, Mr. Speaker, how are we to encourage our young people to pursue their studies in science when the government makes no effort to promote research and development. This is evidenced by the fact that we spend less in that area so vital to our economic progress than any other industrialized country.
This government admits that the Canadian economy needs to be revived. The way to go, according to them, is to negotiate a North America-wide free trade deal. As
The Address
you know, Mr. Speaker, I represent the riding of Saint-Leonard, a riding seriously hurt by the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement. In my riding there is an important manufacturing industry and companies like Maxim Canada Inc. and Rosita Shoes suffered the consequences of this government's disastrous economic policies. How can you expect the Canadian workers to compete with the Mexican workers who earn $2 an hour on average?
Mr. Speaker, the government seems to link national unity to economic prosperity in the Speech from the Throne. I have to say that, if indeed the unity of our country depends on the economic prosperity promised by the Conservatives, we are in serious trouble.
A key factor contributing to national unity, Mr. Speaker, is the promotion and strenghtening of our national identity. Our identity is based on cultural achievements. It is clear that this government does not care as much about this aspect because there is only one short reference to it.
One of the best tool for promoting and strenghtening our identity is the CBC. Unfortunately, the government has closed down stations in Calgary, Saskatoon, Windsor, Comer Brook, Sydney, Matane, Rimouski and Sept-Iles. How can we talk about culture and identity while, at the same time, dismantling a tool that has served us well in that respect? I believe that the task is becoming harder and harder, Mr. Speaker.
This Speech from the Throne, just like the one of April 3, 1989, clearly shows the Conservatives' lack of leadership on the Constitution and national unity. Since the Meech Lake Accord failed, Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives have no constitutional position or platform. Canadians have a government that offers no solution to the country's constitutional deadlock.
The government's answer to this dilemma is to create another committee, Mr. Speaker. Canadians have enough of being studied; they want answers, they want results. This committee is not to report until January 1992. That means Canadians must wait eight more months before finding out the Conservative government's constitutional position.

May 22, 1991
The Address
Once again, Mr. Speaker, this government is waiting till the last minute to solve such an important problem. It is playing poker with Canada's future. It would seem that the government has learned nothing from the failure of the Meech Lake Accord. Every minute that the government lets go by on this issue is wasted time that could have been used to solve the constitutional problems and finally concentrate our efforts on the economy and job creation for all Canadians.
Obviously, the government lacks leadership. However, on our side, Mr. Speaker, my leader, the Hon. Jean Chretien, has shown his real leadership qualities by outlining his approach for solving the constitutional problems.
On April 21 in Montreal, the Liberal leader presented his approach for a constitutional framework based on principles that are fair to Quebec and all of Canada. This approach requires the government to take a stand and make public before June 1, 1991 a concrete reform proposal resulting in a Canada-wide referendum. This referendum would cariy with the support of the three main political parties represented in this House, Mr. Speaker. Of course, if these three parties did not support it, this referendum would be illusory.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote you a passage from the Speech from the Throne that seems to justify the Liberal leader's proposed approach. It is found in the section on national unity and reads as follows: "A constitution should unite a nation. Canadians should be able to see themselves mirrored in their constitution."
That is exactly what the Liberal leader proposes with his winning popular consultation formula. Canadians must be given an opportunity to express their feeling of belonging to this country. What finer way is there is there to help Canadians identify with their Constitution than to have it so directly approved by all citizens?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the leader of the Liberal Party of Canada on his courage in putting forward a concrete constitutional proposal while the country waits another eight months for the government's proposal. Mr. Speaker, the Liberal leader has clearly understood that the time to act is now.
Another point that I would like to raise is the question of Canada remaining a generous society. Those words are from the Speech from the Throne of April 1989. Mr. Speaker, caring means open and accessible. Unfortunately, under the Conservatives, Canada has become far less accessible and caring for its citizens and would-be citizens.
Honourable members know that we have two long lists of people waiting to enter Canada. Some of these people have their spouses already settled here, but they are refused admission into this country, and worse of all, they are refused access to their own families. There are couples who have been living apart for four years, one spouse being here and the other in another country. This is unacceptable, especially from a country which claims to be caring and tolerant. Had we had this policy years ago, Mr. Speaker, you and me would not be here today. So, if we are a caring and tolerant nation, we should open the doors, and allow family reunification. This is another of the fundamental policies of a caring Canadian nation.
Mr. Speaker, as I already pointed out, Canada has become less caring towards its own citizens when it decided to cut programs aimed at the less fortunate among us. The fate of the middle class, the fate of the unemployed in the Montreal area, the fate of the sick do not matter, what counts is big business, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, in the few remaining minutes I would like to talk about Montreal. Last Friday, we learned that Pascal Hardware had gone bankrupt. This bankruptcy adds 2,600 unemployed to the 225,000 already without work in April.
Mr. Speaker, Pascal was a big company for sure, and this is why it made the big news. We put the question in the House and asked the government what policy it was going to put forward, what was it going to do to help those 2,600 workers who lost their jobs, who have no hope left for the future.
But, we tend to forget that many small companies are going out of business every day, that many jobs are lost with the failure of those small companies. No one ever mentions them. But, there are thousands upon thousands of jobs lost every day. And still, as we are facing the worst recession brought upon by this government, here we are, listening the same Throne Speech as in 1989, Mr. Speaker.
May 22, 1991

The Address
As I already asked him earlier today, I would like the Minister of Finance to tell me, what he is waiting for before introducing new measures to revitalize the economy, so Canadians, especially young Canadians, can have faith once again in this country. It is a fact that if there are jobs, and if young people can find hope, we will be able to find a solution to many constitutional problems that plague this country, as any other modem country confronted with important changes, Mr. Speaker.
But, for almost seven years, this government has been rebashing the same speech. It raises interest rates-true, after having raised them, it is slowly starting to get them down-but it is too late, Mr. Speaker. People have lost faith. We just have to look-we just had a long week end, and that is where the tragedy is-never had we seen so many Canadians crossing the border to go shopping, Mr. Speaker. This is very serious.
How many victims are there? I am not only talking about Pascal. How many other victims have there been who are not important enough to be make the headline in our dailies? It still goes on. Why have Canadians lost confidence? Why do they not buy in Canada anymore? Here is the crucial question we must ask ourselves. How can we stimulate our economy if our Canadians people do no longer trust our economical system and our products and if prefer to cross the border. They even charter busses to go shopping across the border.
Every day, my colleagues ask the government some questions. What are its answers? It does not have any. But it is necessary to look at the whole situation, Mr. Speaker. Canadians are fed up with the GST, free trade and high interest rates and the time for good sounding rhetoric and studies is over. The Canadians people, as I was saying earlier, are fed up with studies. They want to see some concrete action, they want to work and they want their children to have hope in this great country of ours.

May 22, 1991
The Address
eligible for the program-this in a region with a population of over 500,000 residents-the factory or business that closes down must have at least 100 employees. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate on the Speech from the Throne. I would like to start by saying how proud I am to represent my constituents in the riding of Joliette in a responsible government that looks to the future.
In 1984, this government inherited a country that was divided, poorly governed and in debt to a dangerous degree. That is why we will probably need more than one generation to correct the deficit problem.
Since 1984, our government has made a number of courageous decisions in order to put the country's finances in order and reduce government spending. We have reduced a government apparatus that had become far too unwieldy and costly. We modified our taxation system to make it fairer and more equitable. We improved our relations with our trading partners, which helped us develop new markets and conclude a free trade agreement with the United States, our principle trading partner. In fact, 70 per cent of our exports go the United States. Thanks to this agreement, we have found new outlets for our goods and obtained more secure markets.
We have updated our structures to improve productivity. One example was our decision to eliminate a hidden sales tax-the manufacturer's sales tax which created unemployment and made our industries less competitive-and replace it with a visible tax that is much fairer because it protects the neediest through a system of regular refunds. This is one more example of this government's determination to put the country in a better position to meet increasingly strong competition on external markets. We embarked on deregulation and privatization to make our domestic market more competitive and more productive.
In 1984, we started implementing a strategy for improving our competitive position, and we did so successfully. Of all industrialized countries, comparatively speaking, Canada has created the most jobs and has attracted unprecedented levels of private foreign investment.
All these structural reforms do not necessarily produce tangible results overnight. However, we know the result will be increased productivity in the years to come, for the greater benefit of Canadians. However, we cannot stop there. There is still a lot to be done to achieve the prosperity we want for ourselves and for future generations.
The Speech from the Throne tells us how.
North America-wide free trade is the logical next step if an acceptable agreement can be negotiated with Mexico and the United States.
We will have to maintain controls on government spending. Steps will be taken to cap federal program spending. Legislation will also be introduced so that all GST revenues as well as monies from further privatization of Crown corporations will be used to reduce the national debt. And I think, Mr. Speaker, that this meets the expectations of the people.
We will work with provincial governments to eliminate interprovincial trade and investment barriers by 1995.
We are also planning to generate 2.5 million new jobs over the next nine years, while raising the real incomes of Canadians by 25 percent by the year 2000. That will require the cooperation of business, labour and the various levels of government.
May 22, 1991

However, all these efforts will not produce the expected results if we keep putting all our energies in a debate over constitutional issues. Since the Constitution was patriated in 1982 without Quebec's consent, our national unity has been in jeopardy.
All my government's efforts to rectify this situation and bring Quebec back to the constitutional table were sabotaged. The proposal which was signed by all the provinces would have allowed us, had it been ratified, to undertake with much more serenity the thorough reform the entire Canadian population wishes. Unfortunately, that is not the case.
Therefore we must do all we can now, in that difficult context, to overcome all obstacles, dispel the people's doubts and ready Canada to go forth with confidence into the 21st century. We must do so while protecting the rights of all Canadians. Throughout the country, Canadian men and women must be able to identify with their Constitution and recognize in it their hopes and aspirations. That is why our approach relies on public consultation. And that is what we are doing now with the Citizens Forum and the Beaudoin-Edwards Parliamentary Committee.
And we will continue to consult the public through a parliamentary committee when we will deposit our propositions in the fall. Our propositions will have to reflect Quebec's unique or distinct character as well as the special interests of all the regions of our country. They will have to be based on fairness and efficiency.
Mr. Speaker, any commitment must necessarily be based on a reasonable compromise and conciliation. To reach the objective of a more united and more prosperous Canada, we will need the cooperation of every Canadian man and woman of goodwill who will show tolerance, generosity and fairness.
Economic prosperity is first of all a matter of human resources. While entering a knowledge era, our quality of life will depend on the quality of our knowledge.
In the Speech from the Throne, we are made aware of the fact that four out of ten Canadian adults cannot read or do math well enough to perform everyday tasks. Three out of ten students dropout of high school before graduating.
The Address
Mr. Speaker, my government recognizes that education is a provincial responsibility and respects that fact. But, if we do not act to change that situation, at the beginning of the next century, one third of our people will have no jobs to ensure our prosperity.
Canadians are concerned about these statistics and expect their elected members to propose ways to tackle this problem. That is why our government has included in the Throne Speech goals to cut, by the year 2000, illiteracy rates in half, to ensure that 90 percent of Canadians attain high school diplomas by age 25, and to double the number of post-secondary graduates in mathematics, sciences and engineering.
Of course, we want to pursue these goals within the jurisdictions of the provinces, but with their cooperation.
Canadian industry spends half as much on training its employees as American industry does, a fifth as much as the Japanese and an eighth as much as the Germans.
We have to close the gap. The governement establishes for himself the goal of quadrupling the training provided by employers to their employees. Mr. Speaker, if we want to ensure prosperity for future generations, we must resolutely follow that path.
Mr. Speaker, I do not have enough time to expand on what the government proposed in the Speech from the Throne to do for the environment, the family, the handicapped and the natives.
However, I can assure you and my constituents that I will continue, under the leadership of our Prime Minister, to work with courage and determination for Canada's unity in the greatest respect of the aspirations of our peoples.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words this evening concerning the Speech from the Throne, a speech aimed primarily at finding a way to solve our national unity and constitutional crisis, a crisis which most certainly concerns two fundamentally different visions of Canada. On the one hand is a vision based on the concept of the two founding nations, on the other hand is a vision based on the concept of equality-equal-

May 22, 1991
The Address
ity for all Canadian cultural origins, equality for all 10 provinces, and equality for all Canadians.
For a very substantial number of English-speaking Canadians, at least, this crisis goes well beyond the Quebec issues. It also involves the concerns of native Canadians, of women, Canadians whose heritage is neither English nor French, national standards, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, multiculturalism and our system of government itself.
It is veiy much a crisis of confidence in our present system of government. Those feelings were clearly evident in the Meech Lake debate, and again, they are now very clearly evident in the findings of the Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future. However, in the face of this lack of confidence and trust in our present system, both the minister of constitutional affairs and the Prime Minister have said that we are going to solve our unity and constitutional crisis by using the very system that so many Canadians do not trust to represent their interests. That is, the present House of Commons and the present Senate.
With the greatest of respect, that will not solve this crisis. When the minister of constitutional affairs says, as he did last week in this House, that members of this House and members of the Senate will solve this crisis in, and I quote: "the most open and innovative way", does he truly believe that the real decisions are going to be made here in this House in an open way, and not by the Prime Minister behind closed doors?
When the Prime Minister said last week that there is no greater constituent assembly than the House of Commons, and that the House of Commons will assume national leadership, did he really believe that the members of this House would assume the leadership role in this crisis rather than he, himself, as the Prime Minister of this country?
If the press and the media truly believed that the House of Commons will assume the national leadership role in this crisis, would the Press Gallery not be packed tonight? It is not. They were here for the speech of the Prime Minister and for the party leaders. They are not here now.
If there truly is no greater constituent assembly than this House of Commons, should Canadians not be hearing their members of Parliament in this very crucial debate deal with the issues that Canadians have raised
before the Citizens' Forum in an open and an innovative way?
It is no wonder, then, that so many Canadians have no confidence in the ability of this House or its members to speak for them. That is why Canadians want to be involved in this process themselves. That is why we need a truly representative constituent assembly, one that Canadians will have confidence in, one that truly speaks for them, and that they feel truly speaks for them.
Ideally, such an assembly should be directly elected and made up of men and women, native Canadians and Canadians born elsewhere, represented proportionately and geographically as they appear in Canadian society itself. It would be very difficult within the time set for the Quebec referendum by the Belanger-Campeau report to design geographic constituencies for an elected assembly which accurately reflect the demographics of Canada. It is quite possible to establish a non-elected but representative constituent assembly within such a time frame.
The 1991 Canadian census will be carried out on June 4. By mid-Januaiy 1992 we will know the present demographic and geographic composition of our country. At that time all Canadians interested in sitting as a member of the constituent assembly could file an application, pay a deposit and submit nomination papers signed by at least 200 persons from the demographic and the geographic category that he or she wished to represent in the assembly.
Two hundred and ninety-five of the applicants, the same number as the present number of federal constituencies, would then be chosen by computer, as suggested by former Supreme Court Justice Estey, to constitute a representative assembly as reflected by the 1991 census. Present politicians would be eligible to apply but they would have no better chance of selection by the computer than any other Canadian.
The assembly would convene 30 days after its selection, choose its own chairperson, establish its own procedure, consider all submissions, concepts, ideas that were presented to it in writing and make its constitutional recommendations to Parliament four months later, just as the United States constituent assembly in Philadelphia did in 1787.
These recommendations would then be subject to ratification by all Canadians in a federally sponsored referendum, tabulated on a province-by-province basis. This would ensure that all Canadians were involved in
May 22, 1991

the constitutional process and that their feelings were made clear to this Parliament and to the provincial and the territorial legislatures.
The recommendations and the results of the referendum would then be submitted to Parliament and to the 10 provincial legislatures to be dealt with in accordance with the amending formula of our present 1982 Constitution Act. This approach would ensure that Canadians get the Constitution that they want and not the Constitution that we, the politicians, want them to have.
It has been said that Quebec will not participate in a constituent assembly. Mr. Remillard has said so publicly. To the best of my knowledge, Premier Bourassa has not. Premier Bourassa has said that he will not talk to anyone else but the federal government and that it is unacceptable to Quebec to talk to the other provinces. It is just as unacceptable to Canada that Quebec talk only to the federal government, a federal government and a Parliament that it really does not trust.
The only real solution is a truly representative constituent assembly in which we all participate. If Quebec refuses, the constituent assembly can be used to develop Canadians' response to Quebec, a response that Quebec tells us it is waiting for.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this important debate.
Apart from the over-arching importance of the need for Canadian unity, the section of the Speech from the Throne of particular personal interest to me is the section on participating in prosperity. In particular, this section places appropriate emphasis and federal government attention in human resource development and in the field of education.
In the area of human resource development, the speech rightfully notes that in the interdependent world we live in prosperity will, more and more, be a factor of knowledge, skills and innovation. Increasingly-thanks for the support back here-economic prosperity is first
The Address
and foremost an issue of the people. Canada's ability to prosper in a global economy will be determined by the level of Canadians' educational achievement, by the sophistication of our management skills and by our attitudes to work and to change.
Globalization requires a new strategic alliance between government, labour and business. It means striking new effective partnerships, new forms of co-operation and collaboration between all major stakeholders if we are to meet the challenge of the integrated global economy.
While technology is certainly an important component of competitiveness, it is not by itself sufficient. A high quality work force and organizational innovations are required to capture the full potential of the new technologies that are around us.
The message is clear: Canada needs to build on its past performance in human resources to maintain its high standard of living and to ensure prosperity for future generations.
Canada ranked third, after the United States and Japan, out of 23 OECD countries, in terms of its human resources according to the 1990 edition of The World Competitiveness Report. Canada did poorly, however, in areas such as managerial initiatives, 15th; vocational training, 16th; and availability of skilled labour, 15th. These areas are now, more than ever, of key importance to competitiveness in Canada.
While Canada's education and training systems have served us well in the past, it is not clear that our systems are geared to meet the new job requirements of the emerging global economy. Nor is it clear that they can respond to demands for continuous learning and retraining brought about by a technology-driven, rapidly changing system.
If we are to meet future competitiveness challenges, we will need to increasingly view the development of human resources as an investment as opposed to a cost item.
The thrust of the Speech from the Throne is that the potential for gains in productivity, flexibility and responsiveness offered by the new technologies can only be realized through the skill and innovation that workers and management bring to their adoption and to their use.

May 22, 1991
The Address
It has been said that intelligent machines work best when paired in innovative ways with skilled workers. In this light, the challenge for all major stakeholders is to craft a way that ensures new workers entering the labour force of the capability to learn new skills many times in their working lives. Once they are in the labour force, they will probably have to be retrained a number of times. So they should be encouraged to learn new skills, to accept new challenges and job changes.
The Speech from the Throne is essentially about preparing us for the 21st century. For example, it is about developing a strong training culture in this country and continuing to move toward a more active training system than one that is based strictly on income maintenance. Our wealth and resources, both material and human, have led us to a point of complacency about the importance of skilled and innovative workers that must be drastically altered if we are to meet the challenge of a knowledge-driven economy.
In the wake of strong growth in the labour force over the past several decades, we have developed a weak training culture and thus have failed to adequately recognize that investment in human resource development is just as important as investment in plants and equipment. So we must do these things to be competitive.
The demographers tell us that by the year 2040, Canada will change from a country with abundant labour and scarce capital to a country with scarce labour and abundant capital.
Throughout the 1990s it is anticipated that the labour force will grow at a slower rate than in the previous two decades. It will grow at only an average of 1.2 per cent. What does this mean to Canada? It means we must put greater reliance on the current labour force and the pressures of adjustment will affect the existing work force much more directly than in the past.
Predictions of future job prospects also tell us that more and more will require higher skill levels with the growth of this information-based society. Fuelled by changes in technology and economic restructuring, Canadians have begun to witness the occupational transformation which is occurring in this country. We have experienced a shift from primarily a goods economy to a service economy. The problem arises in that there will be
a general increase in the skill content and education requirements in most occupations and many future jobs will require higher skills.
Almost half of the jobs created between 1990 and 2000 will require more than five years of combined education and training beyond the completion of high school. The problem is that these requirements will exceed the current education and training levels of many workers.
Some 60 per cent of the workers today possess no more than secondary school education. In the absence of action there could be an increasing mismatch between the skills available and those that will be in demand. In the end Canadian industry and our economic prosperity depend upon a flexible workforce capable of taking on new jobs, changing occupations, acquiring new knowledge and developing new skills.
As we emerge as an information-based society, the need to adapt to the new skill demands on a regular basis will affect increasingly the number of Canadians. In tomorrow's society our workers will have to maintain a core of specific occupational skills, i.e. literacy and numeracy. They have to access skills up-grading and will need to be multi-skilled.
In effect, workers will increasingly be required to undertake a lifetime of learning in the work force. The convergence of these demographic and technological trends raises important questions about how well equipped we are to maintain and improve on our relatively high standard of living in Canada. For example, as envisaged in the Speech from the Throne, an important vehicle or mechanism through which the problem of skills-training can be addressed is our education system.
In the field of education, the speech correctly notes that in the dawning knowledge age how well we live will depend on how well we learn. Canadian men and women must have access to both the skills and the life-long learning opportunities necessaiy to improve their job prospects and ensure their prosperity.
Like our approaches to training and human resource development, our education system is under pressure to reform its curriculum so as to better prepare students to contribute effectively to a rapidly changing knowledge and technology intensive economy. There appears to be considerable agreement that schools should provide
May 22, 1991

students with the basic skills they will need for a lifetime of learning so they can be trained and retrained.
Canada is near the top of the OECD countries in terms of spending on education. Currently Canadians are investing some $50 billion in education and training systems, $45 billion in formal education, and $5 billion in adult training. The federal government spends over $10 billion a year in education, a terrific amount of money, but it raises some great concerns about the results.
Despite the high levels of money poured into it the current education system produces something short of world-class results. The commitment to a discussion paper on learning is not intended, as noted in the throne speech, to violate provincial jurisdiction. That is set out or acknowledged in the speech itself. It is looking beyond jurisdictional squabbling to what is good and best for the country as a whole.
This is a commitment targeted toward a system apparently in need of direction and reform. The question is seemingly one of quality in education. Our education system is facing challenges.
The discussion paper will be out in a short while. All Canadians will be asked to participate and we will be looking forward to setting some new directions in education, as we have noted in this speech and in the throne speech, which are so needed for the development of our people so that we keep them in our schools, reduce the drop-out rate from our high schools and reduce this business of 17 per cent functional literacy and numeracy on graduates.
We are looking forward to important results from this discussion paper so we can carry on in developing our human resources in Canada. We must move in to the 21st century in the right way so that we maximize our prosperity in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after nearly seven years in office, this government has brought in a throne speech which was heralded as the most critical and important in Canadian history.
The Address
While we have heard about the need for new ideas, we can find few new ideas in the path the throne speech has laid out.
There were some positive signals, however, although they were vague.
First, there is no doubt about the importance of eliminating interprovincial trade barriers to ensure Canadian competitiveness. The Reform Party has advocated this for some time. It is hard to imagine an economic policy which has free trade with the U.S. without free trade within Canada. However, it has taken a long time to realize that problem.
Second, regarding the call to improve education and training, there is little doubt of the need for Canada to do this to ensure economic prosperity. However, defining the problem is not a prescription.
Third, the government description of the changes in the way Ottawa works are almost directly out of the Reform Party manual and were a primary reason for my party's creation. However, one has to ask whether description of problems equals the will to change. If Canadians want reform of interprovincial trade, education system and the Parliament of Canada, they certainly need to send reformers.
Of all the issues facing Canada, the issues of national unity and constitutional change are the ones which are to be of key importance in this session of Parliament and to Canadians outside these walls.
Our ability to settle the fundamental question of Canada's unity will decide whether Canada enters the 21st century on a sound footing as a united country or whether it staggers into the next millennium still seeking solutions to problems that have gone unanswered.
For the record, the Reform Party proposes that the Constitution of a new Canada ought to be built on the following basis:
First, new Canada ought to be built by those who want in. Canada should not be built by accommodating those who wish to divide it in order to remain united.
Second, new Canada ought to have a genuinely federal system, including a strong national government with strong regional representation through a Triple E Senate

May 22, 1991
The Address
and strong provinces to protect cultural identity and regional character.
Third, new Canada ought to have a division of power which fulfils the needs Canadians share, especially the needs for a competitive economy, a sustainable environment and a responsible community.
Fourth, new Canada ought to be a country which respects the democratic values that Canadians share and protects the interests of Canadians in the current constitutional situation. It ought to have a new Constitution which is accepted by demonstrated popular consent. It should not be a federation where powerful interests succeed in getting their ideology entrenched in the Constitution of Canada so the public cannot choose a new course even if it wanted to.
In summary, the Reform Party believes that new Canada should be a balanced democratic federation of provinces, distinguished by the conservation of its magnificent environment, the viability of its economy and recognition of the equality and uniqueness of all its citizens and provinces.
In the 12 months since the defeat of Meech Lake, the Reform Party has put forth its view. The Liberals, NDP and various provincial governments have also put forth their views on future constitutional development. The federal government has yet to put forward any concrete constitutional proposals of its own.
Almost a year after Meech Lake we have had hearings, committees, forums, the Prime Minister's committee of committees, the promise of more committees, and yet no concrete proposals of where the government actually stands on this issue.
We have been given vague proposals and high-sounding platitudes, talk of economic costs and benefits, but no vision of exactly what the government wants for this country, except that it remain united, which most Canadians, including myself and the Reform Party desire as well.
Certainly, one of the major reasons that Meech failed to win public support was the top-down, closed-door process. From the Reform Party's perspective, if the process is not correct, there is little chance that the content will bear the public's approval. The process followed is as important as the content, because the proper process will ensure that the content is good for Canada and acceptable to the Canadian public.
It is almost unprecedented for a government which has lost the confidence of the Canadian public and has already seen its major constitutional agenda fail to announce its intention to keep control of the entire constitutional process in upcoming negotiations before obtaining a new mandate.
While all of us who sit in this House have a constitutional responsibility to deal with major areas of concern to Canada, it is an undeniable fact that the parliamentary institutions and individuals are held in some degree of contempt by the Canadian public. This undermines the ability of Parliament and the government to propose even truly good constitutional changes to a suspicious public.
If the old Canada parties close ranks, the public will think they are trying to put something over on them. If the old Canada parties act on partisan lines, then the public is just as likely to consider it to be political posturing.
Reformers believe that the process of constitutionmaking in Canada must be as open and as broadly based as possible. Even before Meech, the Reform Party was a strong advocate of constituent assemblies, a concept which has very much come into vogue.
Of course, we would like to see a process involving directly elected delegates to these assemblies held on a provincial or regional basis as well as one held for aboriginal people.
Reformers believe that aboriginal people should be given the opportunity to define among themselves their position in the new Canada, their relationship to the federal government, and their rights and responsibilities, and not merely to have their conditions simply studied further.
Reformers believe that constitutional conventions held on a provincial or regional basis before a national convention is convened help to ensure that the hopes and aspirations of all provinces are put forward. This will help to ensure that the best opportunity to reach consensus is reached.
Many Canadians are suspicious of a call for a single national convention before each region has had time to develop its position and, for that matter, of the Prime Minister's insistence that the the House of Commons, with 50 per cent of its seats representing only two provinces, deal with constitutional negotiations on behalf of an entire federation.
May 22, 1991

Reformers believe that ordinary citizens would best be able to stand for an election to a constituent assembly. While Canadians recognize the hard work and dedication of their elected officials, they also recognize their very partisan nature, the excessive party discipline and the deeply held ideological bias of many elected representatives, characteristics which most Canadians simply do not share. This leaves Reformers to prefer a non-political, non-partisan convention.
Also, the short-run vision of our politicians to gain electoral success contrasts with Canada's need for a long-lasting Constitution and united country.
Of course, Reformers believe that once a constitutional package has been developed by a constituent assembly and ratified by the elected provincial legislatures and Parliament, it should be ratified by a referendum of each province.
Reformers believe that a constitution developed in a bottom-up process with a constituent assembly at the front end followed by a referendum is the best way to achieve the consensus which Canada needs and which Canadians are now demanding.
When Canadians and Reformers speak of consensus, they mean a consensus of the people of Canada, not the traditional mythical consensus of old Canada's politicians, which was a consensus of political elites, the Canadian establishment and other people who matter.
Old Canada's supporters will say that consensus cannot be worked out if too many people are involved. Certainly, this is a slightly warped view of what true consensus is. Consensus, it is said in old Canada, can only be worked out in secret and behind closed doors. Compromise in old Canada can only be achieved when a majority government can force through compromise when it cannot achieve consensus. Compromise in new Canada can only be worked out through a genuine process of give and take, where each side is involved.
Reformers believe that, free of threats or ultimatums, the process of a constituent assembly and a referendum is the best way of assuring that genuine compromises are developed and reached so that each region has an opportunity to ensure that their hopes and aspirations are addressed and embodied in the Constitution.
The Address
A constitutional package developed in a public consensus-building process, as the Reform Party has suggested, stands the best possibility of being a deal that will bear the will of Canadians and of being a package that will withstand the test of time.
If, however, this constitutional package is reached by bullying threats and coercion, especially over economic circumstances, if a deal is developed as the result of panic to meet a deadline or an ultimatum or else Canada will not survive, if a deal is reached that is perceived, like the 1982 Constitution, to exclude a province or region of Canada, or if a deal is perceived to be for the benefit of one province and the exclusion of the others, like the 1987 accord, if the deal finds accommodation without finding solutions to deeper underlying problems, if it addresses the concerns of one group and excludes others, if it is a deal where people are spoken to but neither listened to nor understood because of a top-down process, then the deal reached will either fail or only be a temporary solution that will help only to inflame underlying tensions and divisions.
It will ensure that Canada stumbles into the 21st century, uncertain about its future, its direction and its unity.
For three decades various political leaders and political parties have proposed solutions to Canada's problems. They have not solved our problems, and in many cases have not even addressed the real problems.
One of the primary reasons Canada's major problems, especially those concerning Quebec have yet to be answered is that Canadian politicians have failed to believe, or comprehend, the honesty of some positions taken.
It has often been said that Canada should not separate because we have built a country that is the envy of the world. Canadians all know that Canada is a country worth preserving, and Reformers have always said that we want to preserve Canada as one country if possible; however Canada cannot continue to be a house divided against itself.
Almost 2,500 years ago there came into existence a great confederation which produced a golden age which was the envy of the ancient world. Its architecture, philosophers and poets are still held in reverence to this day. At the centre of the confederation of ancient Greece there was a great city surrounded by great walls which no army could breach. Inside these walls was the rich city and culture and the first democracy known to . man. While the confederacy was vast, the democracy was limited to those few who lived within those walls; those living outside the walls began to perceive and those living

within the walls began to believe that the purpose of this confederacy was to build a civilization that would be the envy of the ancient world.
Despite its greatness, the ancient Greek confederacy and its great civilization crumbled because of internal dissension, the result of failing to listen to the hopes and aspirations of the confederation outside the walls of Athens.
Now parallels can be drawn from events of 2,500 years ago. The historian of the great dissolution of that confederation, Thucydides, wrote "The Greeks did not understand each other any longer, though they spoke the same language". Some may say; well, I am speaking of the two major language groups in Canada. However, what some others see in Canada is the inability of the politicians of old Canada, living behind these walls, to hear and to understand the people already living in new Canada.
Finally, a country cannot be founded or maintained merely by threats and fear. Neither can a country be built merely upon the economic benefits to the participants or to make the world envious. Debate about a commitment to Canada should be more than just a discussion about the economic costs and benefits. A country can only be maintained by a clear commitment and a feeling of belonging on the part of all its citizens and all its provinces.

Mr. Speaker, The hon. member spoke about a vision of a new Canada compared to an old Canada. I guess I come from the old Canada and I identify with the old Canada. It has proven to be, in spite of a small population, one of the most prosperous in the world, an old Canada that has carved out a place for itself in the history of the world. It stands as a symbol of what can be done when people come together and work with vision and commitment, a symbol of which it can be said that there is a vision that understands that bigger and stronger is not always better, where compromise is of value and not just confrontation.
I find it peculiar that the Reform Party presents itself as a party of the grass roots, and yet when I sat at my television set and watched their convention I discovered that of all of the parties in this country, it is the Reform Party that is the least grass roots, because one individual stands at the top and spreads his gospel down. I ask the hon. member to respond as to how that happens.
